questions.question: How does Inter-VLAN routing work in 'Router-on-a-Stick' configuration using sub-interfaces compared to hardware-accelerated routing via Switched Virtual Interfaces (SVIs) on a Layer 3 switch?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: describes Router-on-a-Stick: a single physical interface connected to a trunk is split into logical sub-interfaces, each assigned an 802.1Q tag and IP gateway
identifies the bottleneck: traffic between VLANs travels up the link and back down (hairpinning), halving effective trunk throughput
describes Layer 3 Switch SVI: logical routing interfaces configured directly in switch silicon ASIC hardware
highlights the performance advantage: SVIs route packets at line rate / wire-speed without traversing an external router

questions.question: How does Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) map an IPv4 address to a physical MAC address on a local link, and what is the difference between ARP Request and ARP Reply?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that a sender wanting to communicate with an IP on the local subnet queries its local ARP cache first
describes ARP Request: encapsulated in a broadcast Ethernet frame (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) received by all hosts on the LAN
describes ARP Reply: the host owning the requested IP sends a direct unicast frame back to the requester containing its MAC address
explains that both hosts update their internal ARP cache tables with the new IP-to-MAC mapping

questions.question: What is Gratuitous ARP (GARP), and how is it leveraged for duplicate IP detection and high-availability gateway failover (such as VRRP / HSRP)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Gratuitous ARP: an ARP request or reply where the sender IP and target IP are identical
explains duplicate address detection: on interface boot, a host broadcasts a GARP; receiving an ARP reply proves another device is illegally using that IP
explains failover mechanism: when a backup router becomes master in VRRP, it broadcasts a GARP with the virtual IP and new MAC
identifies that connected switches immediately update their MAC address tables to direct traffic toward the new master port without waiting for cache expiration

questions.question: What is Proxy ARP, in what legacy or subnetting scenarios is it useful, and what security vulnerabilities does it introduce?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Proxy ARP: a router answers ARP requests for destination hosts located on a different network, replying with its own MAC address
explains its legacy use: allows hosts configured with flat subnets or missing default gateways to reach remote nodes transparently
identifies drawbacks: increases ARP traffic overhead, inflates host ARP tables, and masks misconfigured subnet masks
identifies security risk: creates inherent susceptibility to denial of service or interception if improperly configured

questions.question: How does an ARP Poisoning / ARP Spoofing attack achieve Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) interception, and how does Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) coupled with DHCP Snooping prevent it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the attack mechanism: attacker sends unsolicited gratuitous ARP replies to victim host and gateway, associating the gateway's IP with the attacker's MAC
explains how victim traffic routes through attacker's NIC for eavesdropping or alteration before forwarding
explains DHCP Snooping: switch monitors DHCP transactions to build a trusted IP-MAC-Port-VLAN binding database
explains Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI): switch intercepts all ARP packets on untrusted ports and drops any packet whose IP-to-MAC mapping does not match the snooping database

questions.question: What is Link Aggregation (IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX LACP), and how does frame distribution hashing across aggregate links avoid out-of-order packet delivery?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that LACP bundles multiple physical Ethernet interfaces into a single logical channel (LAG/EtherChannel) for combined bandwidth and redundancy
explains why round-robin packet distribution across links causes TCP packet reordering and performance collapse
explains hash-based flow affinity: switch computes a hash of packet headers (e.g. source/dest IP, source/dest port) to pin all packets of a TCP conversation to the same physical link
notes that a single TCP flow cannot exceed the bandwidth of a single physical link in the bundle

questions.question: What is the difference between Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) and High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC), and how does PPP perform authentication using PAP and CHAP?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: compares protocols: HDLC is a synchronous bit-oriented standard (often vendor-proprietary on Cisco), while PPP is an open standard supporting synchronous and asynchronous links with LCP/NCP negotiation
explains Password Authentication Protocol (PAP): client transmits username and password in cleartext (insecure)

explains Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP): server sends a random challenge string; client returns MD5 hash of (challenge + shared secret); server verifies without transmitting secret
notes that CHAP performs periodic re-authentication challenges during the session to prevent session hijacking

questions.question: In optical networking, how does Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM) increase fiber capacity, and what is the difference between Coarse WDM (CWDM) and Dense WDM (DWDM)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that WDM multiplexes multiple independent optical carrier signals onto a single optical fiber strand using different laser wavelengths (colors)
defines CWDM: wide channel spacing (20nm), uncooled lasers, supports up to 18 channels over short/metro distances (<80km)
defines DWDM: ultra-narrow channel spacing (0.8nm / 100GHz or 0.4nm / 50GHz), temperature-stabilized lasers, supports 80 to 160+ channels
highlights DWDM compatibility with Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifiers (EDFA) in the C and L bands for multi-thousand kilometer transoceanic links

questions.question: What is Forward Error Correction (FEC), and why is it preferred over Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) on deep-space or high-bandwidth satellite links?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines ARQ as error detection coupled with retransmission requests (ACK/NAK) upon frame corruption
defines FEC as encoding data with redundant error-correcting codes (e.g. Reed-Solomon, LDPC) allowing the receiver to reconstruct corrupted bits without sender interaction
explains that satellite and deep-space links have extreme round-trip times (RTTs from 500ms to minutes/hours), making ARQ retransmissions painfully slow
identifies that one-way broadcast links (satellite TV) lack a reverse channel for ACKs, making FEC mandatory

questions.question: How does the Internet Checksum algorithm (RFC 1071) compute its 16-bit 1's complement sum, and why does it fail to detect swapped 16-bit words or inserted zeros?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the algorithm: data is treated as a sequence of 16-bit integers, summed using 1's complement arithmetic (carrying overflow bits back into the lowest bit), and then inverted
explains receiver verification: summing all words including the received checksum must result in 0xFFFF (or 0x0000 in 1's complement)
explains why addition commutativity prevents detecting reordered or swapped 16-bit words
explains that inserting or deleting blocks of all-zero 16-bit words leaves the arithmetic sum completely unchanged

questions.question: How does Ethernet Flow Control (IEEE 802.3x PAUSE frame) work, and why does pause-frame propagation across a network cause head-of-line blocking and buffer bloat?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that when a receiving switch port's buffer crosses a high-water mark, it transmits a PAUSE frame (opcode 0x0001) specifying a pause duration
explains that the sending link partner stops transmission until the timer expires or a zero-pause frame arrives
identifies the flaw: standard PAUSE halts all traffic on the link, blocking unrelated traffic destined for uncongested ports (head-of-line blocking)
explains how congestion cascades upstream across multiple switches, leading to the development of Priority-based Flow Control (PFC, 802.1Qbb)

questions.question: What is Priority-based Flow Control (PFC, IEEE 802.1Qbb) in Data Center Bridging (DCB), and how does it enable lossless transport for RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCEv2)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that PFC extends standard PAUSE frames by allowing independent pause commands for each of the 8 CoS (802.1p) traffic classes
explains that pausing one priority class (e.g. RoCEv2 storage traffic) leaves other priority classes (e.g. regular TCP/IP traffic) unblocked
explains that RoCEv2 relies on lossless Ethernet to achieve ultra-low latency and bypass kernel software retransmission stacks
identifies challenges with PFC: PFC deadlocks caused by cyclic pause dependency loops across switch topologies

questions.question: What is the difference between Store-and-Forward switching, Cut-Through switching, and Fragment-Free switching in terms of forwarding latency and error propagation?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Store-and-Forward: buffers entire frame, validates FCS/CRC-32 checksum; drops corrupted frames but has highest latency proportional to frame size
defines Cut-Through: reads only the destination MAC address (first 6 bytes) and begins forwarding immediately; achieves lowest latency but forwards corrupted packets
defines Fragment-Free: reads the first 64 bytes (the minimum collision window) before forwarding, filtering out collision fragments (runts) while maintaining low latency
notes that modern datacenter switches use cut-through switching to achieve sub-microsecond port-to-port latency

questions.question: What is MAC Flooding attack, how does it degrade a switch into an insecure broadcast hub, and how does Port Security prevent it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that an attacker uses a tool (e.g. macof) to flood the switch with thousands of bogus source MAC addresses per second
explains the effect: the switch CAM table overflows, forcing the switch to 'fail open' and flood all incoming frames out all ports as unknown unicast
explains that the attacker can then sniff all broadcasted LAN traffic passing through the switch
explains Port Security: limits the maximum number of MAC addresses allowed on a port and triggers actions (protect, restrict, or shutdown/err-disable) upon violation

questions.question: How does QinQ (IEEE 802.1ad / VLAN Stacking) allow telecommunications service providers to transport customer VLANs transparently across a shared metro Ethernet backbone?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that QinQ prepends an outer Service Provider tag (S-TAG, TPID 0x88A8) to the customer's existing 802.1Q tagged frame (C-TAG, TPID 0x8100)
explains that provider core switches forward frames based strictly on the outer S-TAG without inspecting or altering customer C-TAGs
explains that multiple customers can use identical internal VLAN IDs (e.g. VLAN 100) without collision or overlap
describes how the egress provider edge switch pops the outer S-TAG and delivers the original tagged frame to the customer's remote site

questions.question: What is Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) at Layer 2 vs Layer 3, and why does TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) or SPB (Shortest Path Bridging) replace STP in cloud datacenters?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the fundamental limitation of STP: blocks redundant links to prevent loops, wasting up to 50% or more of available datacenter bisectional bandwidth
explains that modern datacenters use multi-tier Clos (Spine-Leaf) topologies requiring active-active forwarding across all redundant links
describes TRILL and SPB: run link-state routing algorithms (IS-IS) at Layer 2, encapsulating Ethernet frames with hop counts (TTL) and shortest-path forwarding
highlights that ECMP distributes traffic evenly across all available paths without blocking any physical link

questions.question: How does Wake-on-LAN (WoL) awaken a sleeping computer using a 'Magic Packet', and what is the exact byte composition of this payload?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that the target computer's NIC remains in low-power standby mode listening for specific broadcast frames
details the Magic Packet structure: 6 bytes of all 1s (0xFFFFFFFFFFFF) followed by 16 continuous repetitions of the target machine's 6-byte MAC address
explains that upon detecting this sequence anywhere in the payload, the NIC asserts a power-management signal (PME) to the motherboard to boot the system
notes that the packet is typically broadcast over UDP (ports 7 or 9) or directly as raw Layer 2 Ethernet frame

questions.question: Why is Auto-Negotiation (IEEE 802.3u / 802.3ab) prone to duplex mismatch failures when one side of a link is set to auto-negotiate and the other is manually hardcoded?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that Auto-Negotiation uses Fast Link Pulse (FLP) bursts to negotiate speed and duplex parameters
explains Parallel Detection: when the auto-negotiating end receives no FLP bursts, it senses the line speed accurately but defaults to Half-Duplex for safety
describes the mismatch: the hardcoded side runs in Full-Duplex (transmits and receives simultaneously), while the auto side runs in Half-Duplex (expects CSMA/CD)
identifies symptoms: high rates of CRC errors, collisions, and specifically 'late collisions' causing catastrophic throughput degradation under load

questions.question: In 802.11 Wi-Fi, what is Beacon Frame Interval, and how does the Delivery Traffic Indication Message (DTIM) manage power saving for battery-constrained mobile stations?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that Access Points periodically broadcast Beacon frames (typically every 100ms) to advertise SSID, timing synchronization, and supported rates
describes Traffic Indication Map (TIM): a bitmap within beacons alerting sleeping stations whether buffered unicast frames await retrieval
explains DTIM (Delivery TIM): a specialized beacon indicating that buffered multicast and broadcast frames are about to be transmitted
explains mobile power saving: stations remain in deep sleep, waking up radio circuits only at the negotiated DTIM interval to preserve battery

questions.question: What is the difference between Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access (OFDMA) in Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines OFDM: splits a radio channel into overlapping orthogonal subcarriers, but allocates the entire channel to a single user per time slot
defines OFDMA: divides the channel into smaller groups of subcarriers called Resource Units (RUs), allowing multiple clients to transmit and receive concurrently in the same time slot
explains that OFDMA reduces contention latency and packet overhead for small, bursty payloads (like IoT, VoIP, and gaming)
contrasts with MU-MIMO: OFDMA splits frequency space, whereas MU-MIMO uses spatial beamforming streams

questions.question: How does the Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer (OTDR) locate faults, splices, and attenuation anomalies along thousands of meters of fiber optic cable?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that the OTDR injects high-power laser light pulses into the fiber and measures backscattered and reflected light intensity over time
explains Rayleigh backscattering: tiny microscopic variations in fiber glass density cause continuous low-level light scattering used to measure linear fiber loss (dB/km)
explains Fresnel reflection: sharp refractive index boundaries (connectors, mechanical splices, open fiber breaks) cause distinct reflective light spikes
derives distance: D = (c * t) / (2 * n), where t is transit time, c is speed of light, and n is fiber refractive index

questions.question: What is the function of the Spanning Tree Topology Change Notification (TCN) BPDU, and why does it cause switches to reduce their CAM table aging time from 300 seconds to 15 seconds?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that when a non-edge switch port transitions to Forwarding or down from Forwarding/Learning, it sends a TCN BPDU toward the Root Bridge
explains that the Root Bridge sets the Topology Change (TC) flag in its outgoing configuration BPDUs across the entire network
explains the effect: all receiving switches temporarily reduce their MAC address table aging timer from default (300s) to Forward Delay time (15s)
explains the purpose: rapidly purges stale MAC port mappings so traffic destined for relocated or rerouted hosts is not blackholed on old links

questions.question: How does Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) in Strict vs Loose mode protect networks against spoofed IP address floods at Layer 3 edge boundaries?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that uRPF inspects the SOURCE IP address of incoming packets against the router's Forwarding Information Base (FIB)
defines Strict Mode: drops the packet unless the FIB contains a route back to the source IP that points out the EXACT SAME interface the packet arrived on
defines Loose Mode: drops the packet only if the source IP has no route at all in the FIB (default route optionally excluded)
identifies that Strict Mode fails in asymmetric routing environments where outbound and inbound traffic paths differ, necessitating Loose Mode

questions.question: In copper Ethernet cabling (Cat5e/Cat6), what is Near-End Crosstalk (NEXT) versus Far-End Crosstalk (FEXT), and how does differential signaling on twisted pairs mitigate electromagnetic interference?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines NEXT: unwanted signal coupling between adjacent wire pairs measured at the same end of the cable as the transmitting signal (more severe due to high signal strength)
defines FEXT: signal coupling measured at the far receiver end of the cable (attenuated by distance)
explains differential signaling: transmits equal and opposite voltage polarities (+V and -V) on the two wires of a pair
explains that external noise affects both wires equally, allowing the differential receiver to subtract the signals, canceling common-mode noise while doubling the desired signal

questions.question: What is the difference between LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol, IEEE 802.1AB) and CDP (Cisco Discovery Protocol), and what security considerations surround enabling discovery protocols on user access ports?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: distinguishes protocols: LLDP is an open vendor-neutral IEEE standard, whereas CDP is a proprietary protocol developed by Cisco
explains their mechanism: periodically broadcast Layer 2 frames containing TLV (Type-Length-Value) attributes advertising device ID, software version, capabilities, and port IDs
identifies the security risk: rogue users or attackers running packet sniffers on access ports can effortlessly map network infrastructure, model numbers, and firmware vulnerabilities
proposes best practice: disable discovery protocols on untrusted edge access ports, reserving them strictly for network device interconnects and IP phones (LLDP-MED)

questions.question: What are the key fields of an IPv4 packet header, and how does the Internet Header Length (IHL) field handle optional headers?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: lists primary header fields: Version, IHL, Type of Service (DSCP/ECN), Total Length, Identification, Flags, Fragment Offset, TTL, Protocol, Header Checksum, Source/Dest IP
explains that IHL is a 4-bit field measuring header length in 32-bit (4-byte) words
explains that the minimum IHL value is 5 (5 * 4 = 20 bytes for standard header without options)
explains that any IP options extend IHL up to 15 (60 bytes max), requiring zero-padding to align on a 32-bit boundary

questions.question: How do the Identification, Flags (DF, MF), and Fragment Offset fields in the IPv4 header coordinate packet fragmentation and reassembly across disparate MTU links?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that all fragments of an original datagram share the identical 16-bit Identification number and source/destination IP
explains Fragment Offset: measured in 8-byte units (blocks of 64 bits), indicating the start position of this fragment's payload relative to the original datagram
explains Flags: DF (Don't Fragment) forbids routers from fragmenting; MF (More Fragments) is set to 1 for all fragments except the final one (MF=0)
explains that reassembly occurs exclusively at the final destination host, which reconstructs the payload using the offset values

questions.question: How does Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) dynamically determine the maximum transmission unit without causing packet fragmentation, and what causes a 'PMTUD black hole'?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the mechanism: source host sends packets with DF (Don't Fragment) flag set to 1
describes router response on an MTU bottleneck: router drops packet and replies with ICMP Type 3 Code 4 ('Fragmentation Needed and DF set'), including its next-hop MTU
explains source adaptation: sender reduces its packet size to match the reported MTU and retransmits
defines PMTUD Black Hole: intermediate security firewalls mistakenly block incoming ICMP Type 3 packets, leaving the sender hanging indefinitely in unacknowledged retransmissions

questions.question: What is the difference between Classful Addressing (Classes A, B, C, D, E) and Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), and why was CIDR essential for preventing global routing table collapse?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Classful boundaries: Class A (/8, 16M hosts), Class B (/16, 65k hosts), Class C (/24, 254 hosts), Class D (Multicast), Class E (Experimental)
identifies the flaw: gross allocation waste (organizations needing 1,000 IPs had to take a full /16 Class B, wasting 64,000 addresses) and explosive routing table bloat
explains CIDR (RFC 1519): replaces fixed boundaries with arbitrary prefix masks (/n notation), decoupling network size from class definitions
explains route summarization/aggregation: enables multiple contiguous network prefixes to be advertised as a single aggregate route, curbing global BGP table expansion

questions.question: Given the IP block 192.168.10.0/24, design a Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM) scheme supporting three departments requiring 60, 25, and 12 host addresses respectively, minimizing wasted IP space.
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: applies host formula (2^h - 2 >= hosts required): 60 hosts requires h=6 (2^6 - 2 = 62) -> /26 mask (255.255.255.192)
allocates Dept 2 (25 hosts): requires h=5 (2^5 - 2 = 30) -> /27 mask (255.255.255.224); assigns 192.168.10.64/27 (usable: .65 to .94, broadcast: .95)
allocates Dept 3 (12 hosts): requires h=4 (2^4 - 2 = 14) -> /28 mask (255.255.255.240); assigns 192.168.10.96/28 (usable: .97 to .110, broadcast: .111)

questions.question: How does the Longest Prefix Match (LPM) rule dictate packet forwarding in a router's routing table, and how do hardware Ternary Content Addressable Memories (TCAM) execute LPM lookups in O(1) clock cycles?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines LPM: when a destination IP matches multiple routing table entries (e.g. 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.1.0/24), the router forwards via the route with the most specific (longest) subnet mask (/24)
explains TCAM architecture: memory cells support three states: 0, 1, and 'Don't Care' (X/mask)
explains parallel comparison: all TCAM entries evaluate the input IP against their stored prefix and mask simultaneously in a single clock cycle
explains priority encoder output: if multiple entries match, the priority encoder selects the highest-priority (longest prefix) match directly

questions.question: Why did IPv6 eliminate the header checksum, in-flight router fragmentation, and broadcast addressing found in IPv4?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains checksum elimination: Layer 2 (Ethernet CRC) and Layer 4 (TCP/UDP checksums) already provide robust integrity; eliminating the IPv4 checksum prevents routers from recalculating checksums at every hop upon decrementing TTL/Hop Limit
explains fragmentation shift: routers drop oversized packets with ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, forcing source hosts to execute PMTUD and fragment end-to-end (avoiding router CPU bottlenecks)
explains broadcast removal: broadcast interrupts every CPU on the LAN; IPv6 replaces broadcast with targeted multicast groups (e.g. solicited-node multicast), improving network efficiency

questions.question: What is the 40-byte fixed header structure of IPv6, and how does the Next Header daisy-chain architecture support optional extension headers?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: lists fixed fields: Version (4 bits), Traffic Class (8 bits, DSCP/ECN), Flow Label (20 bits for flow QoS routing), Payload Length (16 bits), Next Header (8 bits), Hop Limit (8 bits, replaces TTL), Source IP (128 bits), Destination IP (128 bits)
explains Next Header daisy-chain: points to either a transport protocol (TCP=6, UDP=17) or an intermediate extension header (Hop-by-Hop, Routing, Fragment, ESP, AH)
explains that extension headers form a linked list processed in order, allowing modular protocol extensibility without cluttering the base header
notes that intermediate routers ignore extension headers (except Hop-by-Hop options), preserving wire-speed forwarding

questions.question: What are the different IPv6 address scopes and prefixes, and how are Link-Local (fe80::/10), Unique Local (fc00::/7), and Global Unicast (2000::/3) addresses utilized?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Link-Local (fe80::/10): automatically assigned on every IPv6 interface, valid strictly within a single local link/broadcast domain, non-routable across routers
defines Unique Local Address (ULA, fc00::/7, typically fd00::/8): routable across an organization's private enterprise network, analogous to IPv4 RFC 1918 addresses
defines Global Unicast Address (GUA, 2000::/3): globally routable and reachable on the public Internet
defines Multicast (ff00::/8): replaces broadcast for group delivery (e.g. ff02::1 for all nodes, ff02::2 for all routers on link)

questions.question: How does Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) generate a host IPv6 address using Router Advertisements, and what privacy concerns prompted RFC 4941 Privacy Extensions?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the SLAAC process: host sends ICMPv6 Router Solicitation (RS); local router responds with Router Advertisement (RA) containing the /64 network prefix
explains modified EUI-64: host takes its 48-bit MAC address, inserts 0xFFFE in the middle, and inverts the Universal/Local (U/L) bit to form a 64-bit Interface ID
identifies the privacy flaw: because the Interface ID is statically derived from hardware MAC, user laptops can be tracked globally across different public Wi-Fi networks
explains RFC 4941 Privacy Extensions: generates pseudorandom, temporary interface IDs that rotate periodically for outbound traffic while maintaining a stable address for inbound services

questions.question: How does Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) in IPv6 replace ARP using ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation (NS) and Neighbor Advertisement (NA), and what is Solicited-Node Multicast?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that IPv6 eliminates ARP broadcasts; address resolution uses ICMPv6 messages over multicast
defines Solicited-Node Multicast address: formed by prefix ff02::1:ff00:0/104 appended with the lower 24 bits of the target IPv6 address
explains the efficiency gain: Ethernet switches with MLD snooping deliver the Neighbor Solicitation only to the exact NIC listening to that multicast group rather than flooding the entire LAN
describes Duplicate Address Detection (DAD): a newly configured host sends an NS for its own tentative IP; receiving an NA indicates an IP address collision

questions.question: How does the Bellman-Ford algorithm compute shortest paths in Distance Vector routing, and what mathematical recurrence relation defines the distance updates?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: states the Bellman-Ford equation: D_x(y) = min_v { c(x, v) + D_v(y) }, where c(x, v) is cost from x to neighbor v, and D_v(y) is v's estimated cost to destination y
explains the distributed nature: each node maintains a vector of distances to all known destinations and periodically advertises this vector to its direct neighbors only
explains update mechanism: when a neighbor advertises a shorter path to destination y, node x updates its routing table and recalculates its own vector
notes that convergence requires up to V - 1 iterations where V is the total number of routers

questions.question: What is the Count-to-Infinity problem in Distance Vector routing protocols, and how do Split Horizon and Poison Reverse mitigate two-node routing loops?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: describes the failure scenario: if link A-B breaks, router A advertises cost infinity; before update arrives, router C advertises a path to A through B; B mistakenly routes to A via C, incrementing costs incrementally until reaching infinity
explains Split Horizon: a router never advertises a route back out the same interface from which it learned that route
explains Poison Reverse: a router advertises the learned route back out the same interface, but explicitly marks its cost as infinity (16 in RIP)
notes that Split Horizon and Poison Reverse solve two-node loops but fail to prevent multi-node routing loops (e.g. 3-router circular topologies)

questions.question: How does Dijkstra's algorithm calculate shortest paths in Link State routing, and how do Link State Advertisements (LSAs) ensure all routers share an identical Link State Database (LSDB)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains LSA flooding: every router discovers its direct neighbors and link costs, packs this local topology into an LSA, and floods it reliably to all routers across the area
explains LSDB synchronization: through reliable flooding, every router in the area builds an identical global topological map (graph) of the network
explains Dijkstra execution: each router runs Dijkstra's algorithm independently with itself as the root node to compute the Shortest Path Tree (SPT)
explains routing table generation: the computed shortest paths populate the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) with next-hop interfaces

questions.question: Why does OSPF elect a Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) on multi-access broadcast networks, and how does this election curb adjacency overhead?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the scaling problem: on an Ethernet segment with N routers, full mesh adjacencies require N * (N - 1) / 2 adjacencies and duplicate LSA flooding storms
explains DR role: routers form full adjacencies exclusively with the DR and BDR, reducing total adjacencies to 2 * (N - 2) + 1 (linear O(N) scaling)
explains multicast communication: regular routers (DROther) send LSUs/LSAcks to AllDRouters (224.0.0.6); the DR replicates and floods updates to all routers via AllSPFRouters (224.0.0.5)
explains election criteria: highest OSPF interface priority wins; ties broken by highest Router ID (RID)

questions.question: What is the hierarchical role of OSPF Area 0 (Backbone Area), and what happens when an OSPF area becomes physically partitioned from Area 0?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains two-tier hierarchy: all non-backbone areas (Area 1, 2, etc.) must connect directly to Area 0 to prevent inter-area routing loops
explains Area Border Router (ABR) role: forwards Type 3 Summary LSAs between non-backbone areas and Area 0
explains area partitioning: if a non-backbone area loses physical connection to Area 0, traffic between it and other areas is immediately dropped (blackholed)
explains OSPF Virtual Link: a logical tunnel configured across a non-backbone transit area to reconnect a disconnected area or heal a partitioned Area 0

questions.question: What are the characteristics and use cases for OSPF Stub Areas, Totally Stubby Areas, and Not-So-Stubby Areas (NSSA)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Stub Area: blocks external Type 5 LSAs (and Type 4 ASBR summaries), replacing them with an injected default route (0.0.0.0/0) to conserve memory and SPF recalculation
defines Totally Stubby Area (Cisco proprietary extension): blocks both Type 5 external LSAs AND Type 3 summary LSAs; uses single default route for all inter-area and external traffic
defines NSSA (Not-So-Stubby Area): allows an external ASBR inside the stub area; external routes are flooded as special Type 7 LSAs within the NSSA
explains Type 7 to Type 5 translation: the NSSA ABR translates Type 7 LSAs into standard Type 5 LSAs before forwarding into Area 0

questions.question: How does Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4) establish neighbor peering over TCP port 179, and what is the difference between External BGP (eBGP) and Internal BGP (iBGP)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains peering session: BGP establishes a reliable TCP connection on port 179 and exchanges OPEN, KEEPALIVE, and UPDATE messages
defines eBGP: peering between routers in different Autonomous Systems (AS); default TTL is 1 (direct physical link required unless eBGP multihop configured); prepends local ASN to AS-Path
defines iBGP: peering between routers within the same AS; TTL is 255; does NOT prepend local ASN to AS-Path
explains the iBGP split-horizon rule: routes learned via iBGP are never advertised to another iBGP peer, mandating a full mesh of iBGP sessions or Route Reflectors

questions.question: What is the complete sequence of the BGP Best Path Selection algorithm when evaluating multiple candidate routes for the same prefix?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: evaluates in strict order: 1. Highest Weight (local to Cisco router), 2. Highest Local Preference (AS-wide preference), 3. Locally originated route (via network/aggregate command)
continues: 4. Shortest AS-Path length, 5. Lowest Origin code (IGP < EGP < Incomplete)
continues: 6. Lowest Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED, received from neighboring AS), 7. Prefer eBGP over iBGP path
tie-breakers: 8. Lowest IGP metric to next hop, 9. Oldest eBGP route (stability), 10. Lowest neighbor BGP Router ID

questions.question: How do network engineers use AS-Path Prepending, Local Preference, and MED to steer inbound and outbound BGP traffic in multi-homed enterprise networks?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Outbound control using Local Preference: set higher Local-Pref on primary ISP uplink to force all outgoing internal traffic to exit through that ISP

explains Inbound control using AS-Path Prepending: artificially append local ASN multiple times (e.g. '65001 65001 65001') in BGP updates to backup ISP, making the backup path appear artificially longer and less desirable to external networks
explains Inbound control using MED (Metric): advertise lower MED to an upstream ISP across multiple peering links to signal the preferred ingress point
notes limitations: external Autonomous Systems can override MED or AS-Path policies using their own upstream Local Preference rules

questions.question: Why do large autonomous systems deploy BGP Route Reflectors (RR) or AS Confederations instead of maintaining a full mesh of internal BGP (iBGP) peerings?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains full mesh scaling barrier: N routers require N * (N - 1) / 2 iBGP sessions (e.g. 100 routers require 4,950 sessions), overwhelming router memory and CPU
explains Route Reflector role: breaks the iBGP split-horizon rule by reflecting routes learned from RR clients to other clients and non-clients

explains RR loop prevention: appends Originator ID (router ID of route creator) and Cluster List (sequence of visited Cluster IDs); routers discard any reflected update containing their own Cluster ID
defines AS Confederation: divides one massive AS into multiple private sub-autonomous systems communicating via eBGP-like peering while appearing as a single AS externally

questions.question: What is BGP Route Flap Damping (RFD), and how does it prevent unstable flapping links from saturating Internet core routers with update floods?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains route flapping: an intermittent circuit rapidly toggles up and down, triggering repeated BGP WITHDRAW and ANNOUNCE messages across the entire Internet
explains RFD penalty system: assigns numeric penalty points (e.g. 1000 points) to a route every time it flaps
explains suppression: when accumulated penalty exceeds a configured 'Suppress Threshold', the router suppresses the route, refusing to install or advertise it
explains decay and reuse: penalty decays exponentially over time governed by a 'Half-Life' parameter; once penalty drops below 'Reuse Threshold', the route is unsuppressed

questions.question: How does ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) report operational failures, and what are the functional differences between ICMP Type 3 (Destination Unreachable) codes?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that ICMP datagrams carry an 8-byte header (Type, Code, Checksum) followed by the original IP header plus first 8 bytes of the offending datagram to identify the faulting socket
distinguishes Code 0 (Network Unreachable): router has no routing table entry matching the destination subnet
distinguishes Code 1 (Host Unreachable): router has route to the subnet but ARP resolution fails (host is offline or unplugged)
distinguishes Code 3 (Port Unreachable): packet reached destination host, but no application process or service is listening on the targeted transport port

questions.question: How does the 'traceroute' utility map the intermediate routing hops to a target host, and how does the implementation differ between Linux (UDP) and Windows (ICMP)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains core mechanism: sends probe packets with incremental TTL values starting at 1; each router decrements TTL by 1, drops the packet at TTL=0, and returns ICMP Type 11 Code 0 ('Time Exceeded in Transit')
explains how hop RTT is calculated from round-trip time between probe transmission and ICMP error reception
contrasts implementations: Windows `tracert` sends ICMP Echo Request packets (Type 8); Linux `traceroute` sends high-numbered UDP probe packets (ports 33434+)
explains destination termination: Linux receives ICMP Type 3 Code 3 ('Port Unreachable') from the destination host, confirming the final destination is reached

questions.question: What is Network Address Translation (NAT) / Port Address Translation (PAT), and how does a home router multiplex thousands of internal connections through a single public IP?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that internal devices use private RFC 1918 IPs (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) that are non-routable on the public Internet
explains PAT mechanism: router replaces internal Source IP and Source Port with its own public WAN IP and a newly allocated ephemeral port
describes NAT translation table: tracks mappings of (Private IP, Private Port) <-> (Public IP, Allocated Public Port, Destination IP, Destination Port)
explains return packet demultiplexing: incoming packets match the allocated public port, allowing the router to rewrite the Destination IP back to the original internal client

questions.question: What are the four classical NAT behavior types (Full Cone, Restricted Cone, Port Restricted Cone, and Symmetric NAT), and why does Symmetric NAT break STUN peer-to-peer traversal?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Full Cone NAT: once internal (IP:Port) maps to public (IP:Port), ANY external host can send packets to that public port
defines Restricted Cone NAT: external host can send to the mapped public port only if the internal host previously sent a packet to that external host's IP
defines Port Restricted Cone NAT: external host must match BOTH the previously contacted IP and Port

defines Symmetric NAT: allocates a UNIQUE public port mapping for every different destination (IP:Port) contacted; breaks STUN because the public port learned from the STUN server is useless for communicating with a peer, mandating a TURN relay

questions.question: How do STUN, TURN, and ICE collaborate to establish direct peer-to-peer audio/video streaming in WebRTC applications located behind NAT firewalls?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT): client contacts public STUN server to discover its reflexive public IP address and port mapping
explains TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT): fallback relay server used when symmetric NATs prevent direct hole punching; relays media streams at bandwidth cost
explains ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment): coordinates the negotiation; gathers host candidates (local IP), server reflexive candidates (STUN), and relay candidates (TURN)
describes connectivity checks: peers exchange candidate lists via signaling and execute connectivity checks to select the lowest-latency direct path

questions.question: What is Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT / NAT444), what dedicated address block is assigned by RFC 6598, and what operational problems does it cause for hosting servers and geolocation?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines CGNAT: Internet Service Providers place an extra layer of NAT inside the provider core network to conserve scarce public IPv4 addresses across thousands of residential subscribers (NAT444 = customer NAT + ISP CGNAT)
identifies the dedicated Shared Address Space: 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598), preventing collisions with private RFC 1918 subnets
explains operational breakage: subscribers cannot perform port forwarding or host inbound servers (VPNs, game servers, home automation) without public IPs
identifies collateral damage: abuse blacklisting (IP bans on Wikipedia, gaming servers) affects hundreds of innocent customers sharing the same public IP

questions.question: How does Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) forward packets based on short fixed-length labels rather than complex IP routing table lookups?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that MPLS inserts a 32-bit 'shim' header (Label, TC/QoS, S/bottom-of-stack, TTL) between Layer 2 and Layer 3 headers
distinguishes Label Edge Routers (LER / Ingress): inspects IP packet, classifies into Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC), pushes initial label onto stack

distinguishes Label Switch Routers (LSR / Core): performs fast hardware label swapping in LFIB (reads incoming label, swaps with outgoing label, transmits on mapped interface) without parsing IP header
explains Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP): the router immediately preceding the egress router removes the outer label to offload processing from the egress router

questions.question: What is Penultimate Hop Popping (PHP) in MPLS, and why does an egress Label Edge Router advertise an implicit null label (Label 3) to its upstream neighbor?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the problem without PHP: egress LER must pop the MPLS label from the incoming frame AND THEN perform a secondary full IP route lookup in its FIB (double lookup)
explains PHP mechanism: the egress LER advertises an Implicit Null label (Label 3) to the penultimate (second to last) hop router
explains penultimate action: the penultimate router pops the top label before transmitting the packet across the final link
highlights the benefit: egress router receives a standard native IP packet directly, requiring only a single FIB route lookup

questions.question: How does Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP) combined with MPLS enable BGP/MPLS IP Virtual Private Networks (L3VPNs, RFC 4364) across a shared service provider backbone?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF): creates independent, isolated virtual routing tables on Provider Edge (PE) routers per customer
explains Route Distinguisher (RD): 64-bit prefix prepended to customer IPv4 addresses to create globally unique 96-bit VPNv4 addresses, allowing overlapping IP blocks across customers
explains MP-BGP: propagates VPNv4 routes between PE routers along with BGP Extended Communities called Route Targets (RT) that govern import/export into VRFs
explains two-label forwarding: outer MPLS label routes packet through the provider core; inner VPN label tells the egress PE which specific customer VRF and interface to deliver to

questions.question: What is the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP, RFC 5798), and how does it provide high-availability default gateway resilience without client-side reconfiguration?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that a group of physical routers form a Virtual Router assigned a shared Virtual IP (VIP) and Virtual MAC (00-00-5E-00-01-VRID)
explains Master election: router with highest configured priority (1-254, or 255 if owning IP) becomes Master and answers ARP requests for the VIP
describes heartbeat monitoring: Master sends periodic VRRP advertisements (default every 1s) to multicast 224.0.0.18
explains failover: if Backup misses 3 consecutive advertisements (Master Down Interval), it transitions to Master and sends a Gratuitous ARP to update switch CAM tables

questions.question: What is the difference between Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGP) metric types in OSPF (E1 vs E2 external routes)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Type E2 (External Type 2, default): metric is fixed at the external cost advertised by the ASBR, ignoring internal path cost to reach the ASBR
defines Type E1 (External Type 1): metric is the SUM of the external cost plus the internal OSPF cost to reach the advertising ASBR
explains path selection preference: E1 routes are strictly preferred over E2 routes for the same prefix
explains design rationale: E1 is used when multiple ASBRs exist to ensure traffic exits via the closest egress point; E2 is used when external cost vastly outweighs internal transit cost

questions.question: How does Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880) provide sub-50-millisecond failure detection across physical media for routing protocols like OSPF, BGP, and IS-IS?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies routing protocol limitations: standard OSPF/BGP hello timers (10s/30s) take several seconds to detect link failure when hardware carrier-loss signals are absent (e.g. through intermediate switches)
defines BFD: lightweight protocol running rapid microsecond/millisecond heartbeat probes (e.g. every 10ms with 3 misses = 30ms failover)
explains routing integration: when BFD declares session down, it immediately signals registered routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) to tear down adjacencies without waiting for hello timeouts
highlights low CPU overhead: BFD packet generation and verification is often implemented directly in network ASIC or line card hardware

questions.question: What is Anycast routing, and how is BGP Anycast used by global DNS root servers and Content Delivery Networks to provide automatic failover and localized latency reduction?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Anycast: multiple geographically distributed physical servers advertise the identical IP address via BGP from different global network locations
explains routing behavior: Internet routers automatically route client traffic to the topologically closest server instance based on standard BGP path selection

explains resilience and DDoS absorption: if an instance fails, BGP withdraws the prefix and traffic routes to the next closest instance; volumetric DDoS attacks are distributed across hundreds of edge sites
identifies challenge with stateful protocols (TCP): BGP routing shifts during an active TCP connection can steer subsequent packets to a different server instance, resetting the connection

questions.question: How does IPsec Tunnel Mode differ from IPsec Transport Mode in packet encapsulation, security headers, and deployment topology?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Transport Mode: encrypts/authenticates only the IP payload (L4 data); original IP header remains untouched; used for host-to-host secure communications
defines Tunnel Mode: encapsulates the ENTIRE original IP packet (original header + payload) inside a brand-new outer IP header; used for site-to-site and client-to-site VPN gateways
explains Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP): provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity, and anti-replay protection
explains Authentication Header (AH): provides integrity and anti-replay without encryption; incompatible with NAT because NAT rewrites IP headers, invalidating AH checksums

questions.question: What are the two phases of the Internet Key Exchange (IKEv1 vs IKEv2) protocol in establishing IPsec Security Associations (SAs)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Phase 1 (IKE SA / ISAKMP): peers authenticate each other (via PSK or certificates) and execute Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish a secure control channel
explains Phase 2 (IPsec SA): peers negotiate encryption algorithms and session keys specifically used by ESP/AH to protect user data traffic
contrasts IKEv1 modes: Main Mode (6 messages, identity protection) vs Aggressive Mode (3 messages, faster but reveals peer identity)
highlights IKEv2 improvements: combines negotiation into fewer round-trips (4 messages), built-in NAT traversal, and native support for MOBIKE (mobility multi-homing)

questions.question: How does NAT Traversal (NAT-T, RFC 3948) solve the failure of IPsec ESP and IKE across intermediate NAT routers using UDP port 4500 encapsulation?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies the problem: ESP (IP protocol 50) lacks Layer 4 port numbers, preventing standard PAT from mapping multiple internal VPN clients through one public IP; additionally, TCP pseudo-header checksums break when NAT alters IPs
describes NAT detection in IKE: peers send vendor-specific hashes of IP and port during initial handshake; mismatched hashes reveal an intermediate NAT device
explains NAT-T encapsulation: IKE ports switch from UDP 500 to UDP 4500, and outgoing ESP packets are wrapped inside a standard UDP header with destination port 4500
shows that the intermediate NAT device can now translate UDP port 4500 normally without corrupting the encrypted ESP payload

questions.question: What is Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE, RFC 2784), and why is GRE commonly combined with IPsec (GRE over IPsec) for site-to-site WAN connectivity?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines GRE: stateless tunneling protocol (IP protocol 47) that encapsulates a wide variety of network-layer protocols inside IP point-to-point tunnels
identifies IPsec limitation: native IPsec unicast tunnel mode cannot transport broadcast or multicast traffic (blocking OSPF/EIGRP hello packets)
explains GRE over IPsec solution: GRE encapsulates dynamic routing multicast packets into unicast GRE packets; IPsec then encrypts the GRE packet using ESP
notes MTU considerations: GRE header (4-24 bytes) plus IPsec overhead increases total packet size, requiring MSS clamping or MTU adjustments to avoid fragmentation

questions.question: How does Segment Routing (SR-MPLS / SRv6) revolutionize traffic engineering by shifting state from transit routers to packet headers using source routing?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the core paradigm: the ingress node encodes the entire end-to-end forwarding path directly into the packet header as an ordered list of Segment IDs (SIDs)
defines Prefix-SID (node destination) and Adjacency-SID (specific link hop)
highlights operational advantage: intermediate transit routers maintain zero per-flow state and require no signaling protocols (eliminating LDP and RSVP-TE)
contrasts SR-MPLS (uses stack of standard MPLS labels) with SRv6 (uses IPv6 Segment Routing Header, SRH, with 128-bit IPv6 addresses as SIDs)

questions.question: What is Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP-TE) in traditional MPLS Traffic Engineering, and what scalability bottlenecks led to its decline?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains RSVP-TE operation: computes paths using Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF) and signals LSP tunnels by sending PATH and RESV messages across core routers to reserve strict bandwidth
defines soft-state architecture: requires periodic refresh messages to maintain reservations on every intermediate router along the tunnel
identifies the bottleneck: as the number of tunnels scales to thousands across a mesh, periodic refresh overhead and state synchronization saturate router CPU and memory
explains why modern hyperscale networks migrate from RSVP-TE to Segment Routing with centralized SDN path computation

questions.question: What is Differentiated Services (DiffServ), and how do the 6-bit DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) values map to Expedited Forwarding (EF) and Assured Forwarding (AF)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that DiffServ repurposes the IPv4 ToS octet / IPv6 Traffic Class into a 6-bit DSCP field (supporting 64 classes) and a 2-bit ECN field
explains Per-Hop Behavior (PHB): each router along the path examines DSCP to apply specific queuing, scheduling, and drop priorities
defines Expedited Forwarding (EF, DSCP 46 / 101110): low-latency, low-jitter, guaranteed bandwidth service with strict priority queuing, dedicated to VoIP media
defines Assured Forwarding (AF): 4 classes with 3 drop precedence levels each (e.g. AF41 vs AF43), where higher drop precedence packets are dropped first during congestion

questions.question: How does Weighted Random Early Detection (WRED) prevent Global TCP Synchronization in congested router queues?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Tail Drop: when a buffer completely fills, all arriving packets are dropped simultaneously

explains Global TCP Synchronization: tail drop causes hundreds of independent TCP flows to lose packets at the same instant, forcing them all to halve their congestion windows simultaneously and creating severe network throughput oscillation
explains RED/WRED mechanism: monitors average queue size; once it exceeds a minimum threshold, the router begins probabilistically dropping random packets BEFORE the queue fills
explains the effect: only a small subset of TCP flows slow down at any given moment, maintaining high overall link utilization and smooth queue depths

questions.question: What is Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN, RFC 3168) in IP and TCP headers, and how does it signal congestion without dropping packets?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the 2-bit field in IP header: 00 = Non-ECT, 10/01 = ECN-Capable Transport (ECT), 11 = Congestion Experienced (CE)
describes router action: when queue occupancy rises, an ECN-aware router marks ECT packets as CE (11) instead of dropping them
describes receiver action: upon seeing CE mark, the destination TCP stack sets the ECE (ECN-Echo) flag in its returning ACK
describes sender reaction: sender halves its congestion window just as if a packet were dropped, and acknowledges with CWR (Congestion Window Reduced) flag

questions.question: How does Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMPv1, v2, v3) manage multicast group membership between hosts and their local multicast router?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains IGMP role: used by IPv4 hosts to report IP multicast group memberships to adjacent multicast routers
explains IGMPv2 enhancements: adds explicit Leave Group message (sent to 224.0.0.2) and Group-Specific Query, reducing leave latency compared to IGMPv1 timeout expiration
explains IGMPv3 major feature: introduces Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), allowing hosts to request traffic from specific source IPs ('INCLUDE' or 'EXCLUDE' lists)
explains IGMP Snooping: switches listen to IGMP membership reports to forward multicast frames strictly to ports with interested receivers rather than flooding

questions.question: What is Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), and how does it transition from the Rendezvous Point Tree (RPT) to the Shortest Path Tree (SPT)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains PIM-SM premise: assumes receivers are sparsely distributed; routers join multicast groups only upon explicit request
explains Rendezvous Point (RP) role: central meeting point where sources register and receivers initially join via Shared Tree (*, G)
describes the switchover: once the last-hop router begins receiving data from the RP, it learns the actual IP address of source S
explains SPT transition: last-hop router sends a direct (S, G) Join towards the source and a Prune towards the RP, establishing an optimal Shortest Path Tree that minimizes latency

questions.question: How does Multipath TCP (MPTCP, RFC 8684) aggregate bandwidth and provide seamless handover across multiple heterogeneous interfaces (e.g. Wi-Fi and Cellular)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that MPTCP presents a standard TCP socket interface to applications while managing multiple underlying TCP subflows over different physical network interfaces
explains connection handshake: initiates with MP_CAPABLE option in SYN/ACK to negotiate MPTCP support and exchange security keys
describes subflow joining: client initiates additional subflows across other interfaces (e.g. LTE) using MP_JOIN option referencing the master connection token
explains cross-subflow sequence numbering: maintains a Data Sequence Number (DSN) across all subflows to ensure seamless reassembly even if Wi-Fi disconnects mid-stream

questions.question: What is GRE Tunnel Keepalive, and why does an endpoint send a GRE packet whose destination address is the sending tunnel endpoint itself?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies GRE limitation: GRE is inherently stateless, leaving a tunnel interface in the 'up/up' state even if the remote peer is dead, causing blackholing of routed traffic
explains keepalive mechanism: router A constructs an inner IP/GRE packet whose destination is Router A itself, encapsulated inside an outer IP/GRE packet addressed to remote Router B
explains remote peer action: Router B decapsulates outer packet and blindly routes the inner packet back to Router A according to normal IP routing
concludes: receiving its own reflected inner packet proves end-to-end bidirectional reachability without requiring remote configuration

questions.question: What is the IP TTL field mechanism, and how does a traceroute distinguish a real link failure from an intermediate router configured to silently drop ICMP Time Exceeded packets?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains that every router decrements TTL by at least 1; if TTL reaches 0 before reaching destination, packet is discarded and ICMP Type 11 is generated
explains why asterisks (* * *) appear in traceroute: an intermediate router drops the probe or rate-limits/disables ICMP generation, or firewalls block return traffic
explains distinction: if hops AFTER the asterisks respond successfully, the network path is fully healthy (router simply withheld ICMP replies)
explains actual failure: if asterisks continue for all subsequent hops to the end of the trace, a genuine routing loop, link down, or hard packet filter exists

questions.question: How does BGP EVPN (Ethernet VPN, RFC 7432) over VXLAN replace traditional Spanning Tree and flood-and-learn architectures in modern software-defined cloud datacenters?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains VXLAN encapsulation: encapsulates Layer 2 Ethernet frames inside Layer 4 UDP packets (port 4789) with a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI, supporting 16M segments)
explains BGP EVPN role: serves as the centralized control plane; advertises MAC and IP bindings via MP-BGP rather than relying on inefficient data plane unknown unicast flooding
defines EVPN Route Types: Type 2 (MAC/IP Advertisement route for host discovery) and Type 3 (Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag route for BUM replication)
identifies benefits: active-active multi-homing (EVPN ESI), eliminates Spanning Tree loops, and enables live VM/container migration across Layer 3 boundaries

questions.question: What is the structure of the TCP header, and how does the Data Offset field indicate the boundary between TCP header options and payload data?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: lists primary header fields: Source Port, Destination Port, 32-bit Sequence Number, 32-bit Acknowledgment Number, 4-bit Data Offset, Reserved, 9 Flags, 16-bit Window Size, Checksum, Urgent Pointer, Options
explains Data Offset: measures header length in 32-bit (4-byte) words, exactly like IPv4 IHL
states the minimum value: 5 (5 * 4 = 20 bytes for standard base header without options)
explains maximum value: 15 (15 * 4 = 60 bytes max), allowing up to 40 bytes of optional parameters (e.g. MSS, SACK, Timestamps)

questions.question: How does the TCP 3-Way Handshake establish a reliable full-duplex connection, and why are Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs) pseudorandomly generated rather than starting at zero?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: steps through handshake: Client sends SYN with ISN_c; Server replies with SYN-ACK with ISN_s and ACK=(ISN_c + 1); Client completes with ACK=(ISN_s + 1)
explains why SYN consumes one sequence number despite carrying no user payload
explains security risk of starting at zero or predictable counters: attackers can forge spoofed TCP connections by predicting sequence numbers (TCP Blind Spoofing / Kevin Mitnick attack)
explains RFC 6528: modern kernels generate cryptographically secure pseudorandom ISNs based on a 4-tuple hash and internal timer

questions.question: How does a SYN Flood attack overwhelm server connection resources, and how do SYN Cookies mitigate the attack without allocating server memory in the half-open queue?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the attack: attacker sends thousands of TCP SYN packets with spoofed source IPs and never responds to SYN-ACKs, exhausting the server's backlog queue (SYN queue) and dropping legitimate requests
explains SYN Cookies mechanism: server avoids allocating any state or Transmission Control Block (TCB) memory upon receiving a SYN
explains ISN encoding: server encodes connection parameters (timestamp, MSS index, cryptographic hash of 4-tuple + secret key) directly into the 32-bit ISN of the SYN-ACK

explains client response verification: when the legitimate client returns the final ACK, the server extracts and validates the cookie from ACK - 1; only upon valid signature does it allocate memory and establish the socket

questions.question: What is the exact sequence of the TCP 4-Way Connection Teardown, and how does the half-closed connection state allow one direction of data transfer to continue?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: traces the 4 steps: Active closer sends FIN (enters FIN_WAIT_1); Passive closer sends ACK (enters CLOSE_WAIT; active closer enters FIN_WAIT_2); Passive closer finishes sending data and sends FIN (enters LAST_ACK); Active closer replies with ACK (enters TIME_WAIT)
defines Half-Closed state: calling `shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)` signals EOF to the remote peer while keeping the receive channel open to consume incoming responses
explains why teardown requires 4 segments unlike 3-way handshake: TCP is full-duplex, and each direction must be terminated independently by the respective sending application
notes that a passive closer can piggyback its own FIN onto the ACK if it has no data left to send, reducing it to 3 segments

questions.question: What is the purpose of the TIME_WAIT state in the TCP state machine, why is its duration set to 2MSL (Maximum Segment Lifetime), and what risks arise from disabling it via SO_LINGER?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Reason 1 (Reliable termination): ensures the final ACK is delivered to passive closer; if lost, passive closer retransmits FIN, and active closer can still re-send ACK from TIME_WAIT

explains Reason 2 (Ghost packet prevention): prevents stale, delayed duplicate segments from an old connection from being accepted by a brand-new connection reincarnating the exact same 4-tuple socket pair
explains 2MSL duration: allows one MSL for the final ACK to traverse the network, plus one MSL for any retransmitted FIN to arrive (typically 60-120 seconds)
explains SO_LINGER risk: aborting with RST to bypass TIME_WAIT terminates connections abruptly, potentially dropping buffered in-transit data and violating TCP reliability guarantees

questions.question: What is the difference between TIME_WAIT socket accumulation and a CLOSE_WAIT socket leak in high-throughput backend services, and how is each resolved?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: distinguishes origin: TIME_WAIT occurs on the ACTIVE closer (normal TCP state); CLOSE_WAIT occurs on the PASSIVE closer (receiving EOF/FIN from peer)

identifies CLOSE_WAIT cause: application programming bug where the application failed to call `close()` or release the socket after receiving an EOF indicator, causing permanent file descriptor exhaustion
identifies TIME_WAIT symptoms: rapid ephemeral port exhaustion on client/proxy nodes initiating millions of short-lived connections

proposes solutions: for TIME_WAIT, use HTTP connection pooling/Keep-Alive, enable `tcp_tw_reuse`, and increase ephemeral port ranges; for CLOSE_WAIT, fix application code to properly close sockets in `finally` blocks

questions.question: How does the TCP Sliding Window mechanism provide end-to-end flow control, and how does the Window Scale option (RFC 7323) overcome the 64KB limitation of the base header?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains flow control principle: receiver advertises available receive buffer space via the 16-bit Window Size field (`rwnd`), preventing sender from overwhelming receiver memory
calculates base limitation: 16 bits yields maximum window of 2^16 - 1 = 65,535 bytes (64 KB), severely bottlenecking gigabit WANs with large Bandwidth-Delay Products
explains Window Scale option (negotiated during SYN): specifies a left-shift factor 'S' up to 14 bits
demonstrates scaling: true window size = `Window Size * 2^S`, expanding the maximum possible window up to 1 gigabyte (65,535 * 2^14 = 1,073,725,440 bytes)

questions.question: What is the Zero Window state in TCP, how does the Zero Window Probe (ZWP) prevent connection deadlocks, and what is a 'TCP Window Full' condition?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Zero Window: receiver buffer is completely full, advertising `rwnd = 0`, forcing sender to halt all data transmission

identifies deadlock scenario: receiver application later drains buffer and sends window update ACK (rwnd > 0); if this ACK is lost, sender waits forever for window to open, and receiver waits forever for data

explains Zero Window Probe (ZWP): sender runs a persist timer; upon expiration, sends a 1-byte probe segment; receiver drops the byte if buffer full but replies with an ACK containing its current window size
distinguishes 'Window Full': sender has exhausted receiver's advertised window, pausing transmission until in-flight segments are acknowledged

questions.question: What is Silly Window Syndrome (SWS) in TCP, and how do Clark's Solution on the receiver and Nagle's Algorithm on the sender eliminate it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines SWS: pathological state where data is transmitted in tiny chunks (e.g. 1-byte payloads wrapped in 40-byte IP/TCP headers), consuming massive overhead and tanking throughput

explains Clark's Solution (receiver): prevents receiver from advertising tiny window increments; receiver advertises `rwnd = 0` until it can accept at least one full MSS or half of its total buffer space
explains Nagle's Algorithm (sender): if there is unacknowledged data in flight, sender buffers all small user writes until either a full MSS is accumulated or an ACK for pending data arrives
explains how both mechanisms ensure packets are sent in large, efficient MSS-sized blocks

questions.question: Why does the interaction between Nagle's Algorithm and TCP Delayed ACKs cause catastrophic 40ms to 200ms latency spikes in interactive applications, and how does TCP_NODELAY resolve it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Delayed ACK: receiver delays sending an ACK (typically 40ms to 200ms) waiting to either piggyback the ACK on outbound response data or acknowledge two back-to-back full packets

explains the deadlock condition: client performs two sequential small writes (e.g. HTTP header then payload); Nagle sends the first write immediately but holds the second write waiting for an ACK; server receives first write but delays ACK; communication deadlocks until receiver's 200ms delayed-ACK timer expires
explains `TCP_NODELAY`: disables Nagle's algorithm on the socket, forcing the kernel to transmit all written data immediately without waiting for previous ACKs
identifies suitable use cases: low-latency RPCs (gRPC), SSH interactive keystrokes, financial trading, and gaming

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP Flow Control and TCP Congestion Control, and how does the effective transmission window balance 'rwnd' and 'cwnd'?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Flow Control: protects the RECEIVER endpoint from being overwhelmed; governed by `rwnd` (Receive Window) advertised directly by receiver in TCP header
defines Congestion Control: protects the INTERMEDIATE NETWORK links and router buffers from being overwhelmed; governed by `cwnd` (Congestion Window) estimated dynamically by sender
states effective window formula: `Allowed In-Flight Bytes = min(rwnd, cwnd)`
explains that throughput is constrained by whichever bottleneck is narrower: receiver processing speed or network transit capacity

questions.question: How do Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance phases operate in classical TCP (Tahoe and Reno), and what mathematical rules govern the expansion of 'cwnd'?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Slow Start: starts with small initial window (typically 1 to 10 MSS); increases `cwnd` by 1 MSS for every received ACK, resulting in exponential doubling of `cwnd` every RTT
explains Slow Start Threshold (`ssthresh`): point of transition; once `cwnd >= ssthresh`, TCP switches from exponential Slow Start to linear Congestion Avoidance
explains Congestion Avoidance: increases `cwnd` by approximately `(1 / cwnd) * MSS` per received ACK (adding exactly 1 MSS per RTT)
explains AIMD (Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease): probe bandwidth cautiously with linear increase, and back off sharply upon loss

questions.question: How does Fast Retransmit detect packet loss before retransmission timer (RTO) expiration, and how does Fast Recovery maintain pipeline throughput in TCP Reno?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Triple Duplicate ACK: receiver generates duplicate ACKs for every out-of-order segment received; arrival of 3 identical duplicate ACKs (4 total ACKs) signals that a single segment was lost rather than minor packet reordering
explains Fast Retransmit: sender retransmits the missing segment immediately without waiting for the expensive Retransmission Timeout (RTO)

contrasts recovery in Tahoe vs Reno: Tahoe resets `cwnd = 1 MSS` and re-enters Slow Start (destroying throughput); Reno enters Fast Recovery: sets `ssthresh = cwnd / 2`, inflates `cwnd = ssthresh + 3 * MSS`, and sends new packets for each subsequent duplicate ACK received
explains recovery exit: upon receiving a new ACK confirming the retransmitted segment, Reno deflates `cwnd = ssthresh` and resumes linear Congestion Avoidance

questions.question: How does Selective Acknowledgment (SACK, RFC 2018) overcome the performance collapse of cumulative ACKs when multiple packets are dropped within a single window?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies cumulative ACK limitation: standard ACK reports only the highest contiguous received byte; if packets 2 and 4 are dropped in a 10-packet burst, sender has no idea whether packets 3, 5-10 were delivered successfully
explains SACK header option: receiver includes up to 4 non-contiguous SACK blocks (left edge, right edge) in the TCP options field reporting isolated blocks of successfully received data
explains sender advantage: sender retransmits ONLY the precise missing gaps (packets 2 and 4) without retransmitting already-delivered packets or stalling pipeline flow
highlights importance on high-latency satellite and gigabit networks where retransmitting entire windows causes catastrophic throughput drops

questions.question: How does Karn's Algorithm prevent ambiguity in Round-Trip Time (RTT) estimation when measuring retransmitted TCP segments?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Retransmission Ambiguity: when a retransmitted segment is acknowledged, the sender cannot determine whether the incoming ACK corresponds to the original transmission (long delayed) or the retransmission
explains the danger: misinterpreting the ACK causes RTT and Smoothed RTT (SRTT) to become wildly inaccurate, leading to premature retransmission storms
states Karn's Rule 1: do NOT update RTT estimates for any segment that has been retransmitted
states Karn's Rule 2: apply exponential backoff to the Retransmission Timeout (RTO = 2 * RTO) for each failed attempt until a segment is delivered without retransmission

questions.question: How does TCP CUBIC scale congestion window growth on high-bandwidth, high-latency networks (Long Fat Networks), and why does its growth function depend on real time rather than RTT?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies standard Reno flaw: linear increase of 1 MSS per RTT requires hours to recover gigabit pipe utilization after a drop on a 100ms transatlantic link
states CUBIC window formula: `W(t) = C * (t - K)^3 + W_max`, where `t` is elapsed time since last loss, `W_max` is window size before loss, and `K` is time to reach `W_max`
explains Concave phase: grows rapidly at first, flattening out as it approaches `W_max` to safely probe former capacity
explains Convex phase: after lingering at `W_max`, accelerates growth to probe for newly available bandwidth
explains RTT fairness advantage: window growth depends on absolute wall-clock time `t`, allowing flows with disparate RTTs to compete equitably

questions.question: What is Google's BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) congestion control, and how does it prevent bufferbloat by rejecting packet loss as a congestion signal?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies flaw in loss-based algorithms (Reno/CUBIC): they assume loss equals congestion, filling deep router buffers until tail drop occurs, creating massive queuing delays (bufferbloat)
explains BBR model: continuously measures two independent physical properties: maximum Bottleneck Bandwidth (`BtlBw`) and minimum Round-Trip Propagation Time (`RTprop`)
defines Kleinrock's optimum: maximum throughput with minimum delay occurs when in-flight data exactly equals the Bandwidth-Delay Product (`BDP = BtlBw * RTprop`)
explains rate pacing: paces packet transmission directly at `BtlBw`, preventing router queue buildup while maintaining full pipe utilization and drastically slashing latency

questions.question: What is the structure of the UDP header, why does it have only 8 bytes of overhead, and under what conditions can a high-throughput UDP application experience socket buffer drops?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: lists the 4 fields (2 bytes each): Source Port, Destination Port, Length (header + payload), Checksum
explains lightweight nature: connectionless, zero handshake, no sequence numbers, no acknowledgments, preserves datagram message boundaries
explains socket buffer drops: if incoming UDP packet burst rate exceeds application processing speed, kernel receive queue (`SO_RCVBUF` / `rmem_default`) fills completely
identifies consequence: kernel silently drops subsequent incoming datagrams without notifying sender or receiver, necessitating buffer tuning (`setsockopt SO_RCVBUF`) and multi-threaded workers

questions.question: How does the TCP Pseudo-Header provide cross-layer error detection in TCP and UDP checksum calculations?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Pseudo-Header fields: Source IP (4 bytes), Destination IP (4 bytes), Reserved Zero byte (1 byte), Protocol (1 byte, 6 for TCP), TCP Length (2 bytes)
explains inclusion during checksum calculation: pseudo-header is prepended to the TCP segment in memory solely during 16-bit 1's complement checksum computation and discarded before transmission

explains purpose: verifies that the segment was delivered to the EXACT intended destination IP and protocol; if an intermediate router corrupts the IP destination, the TCP checksum validation fails at receiver
explains why NAT must rewrite TCP/UDP checksums: modifying IP addresses invalidates the pseudo-header checksum

questions.question: What is the TCP Maximum Segment Size (MSS), how is it calculated from the link MTU, and how does 'MSS Clamping' prevent packet drops on VPN and PPPoE connections?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines MSS: maximum payload data a host can accept in a single TCP segment (excluding IP and TCP headers)
calculates standard value: on standard Ethernet (MTU = 1500 bytes), `MSS = MTU - 20 (IP header) - 20 (TCP header) = 1460 bytes`

identifies tunnel issue: PPPoE adds 8 bytes overhead (MTU=1492, MSS=1452); IPsec/GRE tunnels add 50-70 bytes overhead; packets with DF bit set exceeding tunnel MTU get dropped if ICMP PMTUD is blocked

explains MSS Clamping: intermediate router intercepts TCP SYN packets and rewrites the advertised MSS option to a smaller safe value (e.g. 1400 bytes), forcing endpoints to send smaller segments that traverse tunnels without fragmentation

questions.question: How does the TCP Timestamps option (RFC 7323) provide Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) and precise Round-Trip Time Measurement (RTTM)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains 10-byte Timestamps option: contains TSval (Timestamp Value set by sender) and TSecr (Timestamp Echo Reply returned by receiver)
explains RTTM: sender calculates exact sample RTT by subtracting TSecr from current time upon receiving ACK, eliminating retransmission ambiguity without Karn's restrictions
explains the PAWS problem: on 10Gbps+ links, 32-bit sequence numbers wrap around in under 3 seconds (faster than MSL=120s), allowing old duplicate packets to match valid sequence windows
