explains PAWS solution: receiver inspects TSval timestamp; any segment arriving with an older timestamp than currently established is immediately discarded as a wrapped ghost packet

questions.question: What is the Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking problem at the transport layer in TCP, and how does it impair HTTP/2 performance across lossy wireless connections?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains TCP abstraction: TCP guarantees a single, strictly ordered byte stream to the application
describes the failure mode: if packet N is lost, the kernel buffers packets N+1, N+2... and refuses to release them to application space until packet N is retransmitted and acknowledged
explains impact on HTTP/2: HTTP/2 multiplexes dozens of independent logical request/response streams over a single shared TCP connection

identifies the paradox: a single lost packet belonging to Stream A stalls ALL unrelated streams (Stream B, C, D) on the connection, making HTTP/2 perform worse than HTTP/1.1 on lossy Wi-Fi/cellular networks

questions.question: How does QUIC (RFC 9000) resolve transport-layer Head-of-Line blocking by implementing independent stream state machines over UDP?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains UDP substrate: QUIC runs on top of UDP, entirely bypassing kernel TCP byte-stream ordering constraints
explains independent stream framing: QUIC packets carry STREAM frames with distinct Stream IDs and per-stream offset counters
explains loss isolation: if a packet carrying data for Stream 1 is lost, the receiver delivers incoming data for Stream 2 and Stream 3 to the application immediately without waiting
identifies that retransmission applies strictly to the lost stream offset, eliminating cross-stream head-of-line blocking entirely

questions.question: How does QUIC achieve 0-RTT Connection Establishment, and what replay attack vulnerabilities exist during the 0-RTT window?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: contrasts standard latency: TCP (1 RTT) + TLS 1.3 (1 RTT) requires 2 round trips (or 1 RTT resumed) before sending application data
explains QUIC 0-RTT: client reusing a previously established connection ticket sends encrypted application data ('Early Data') alongside the very first connection packet

identifies Replay Attack danger: an eavesdropper can capture and replay 0-RTT packets; because server has not yet exchanged fresh ephemeral nonces, server may re-execute duplicate requests (e.g. duplicating financial transactions)
proposes defense: restrict 0-RTT strictly to idempotent HTTP methods (GET/HEAD) and utilize server-side anti-replay strike registers or single-use tickets

questions.question: How does Connection Migration in QUIC maintain uninterrupted video streaming and downloads when a mobile device switches from Wi-Fi to cellular data?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies TCP failure: TCP connections are strictly bound to the 4-tuple (Src IP, Src Port, Dst IP, Dst Port); switching from Wi-Fi to 4G/5G changes the IP, immediately breaking active TCP sessions
explains QUIC Connection ID (CID): connections are identified by an opaque 64-bit to 160-bit CID in the QUIC header, decoupled from IP and UDP port
describes migration process: when client switches interface, it transmits from the new IP using the existing CID
explains Path Validation: server receives packet from new IP, issues a PATH_CHALLENGE frame containing random data, and verifies client's PATH_RESPONSE before rerouting data traffic

questions.question: What is TCP Keepalive, how do its configuration parameters (time, interval, probes) operate, and how does it detect dead peers across stateful firewalls?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains role: TCP has no heartbeat by default; an idle connection without traffic consumes zero bandwidth and can remain open indefinitely unless keepalives are enabled
defines `tcp_keepalive_time`: duration of complete connection inactivity before the first keepalive probe is sent (default 7200 seconds / 2 hours)
defines `tcp_keepalive_intvl` and `probes`: interval between probes (e.g. 75 seconds) and number of unacknowledged probes (e.g. 9) before closing the connection with ETIMEDOUT
explains stateful firewall preservation: periodic probes prevent intermediate NAT gateways and stateful firewalls from evicting idle translation table entries

questions.question: How does the TCP Reset (RST) flag operate, what triggers its transmission, and how do malicious actors exploit it in 'TCP RST Attacks' to terminate active sessions?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains legitimate RST triggers: packet arrives for an unlistening port, connection aborted via `SO_LINGER(0)`, or segment arrives with invalid sequence number on half-open connection
explains effect: receiving endpoint immediately destroys its TCB state and closes socket without 4-way teardown
explains TCP RST Attack: an attacker sniffing traffic or guessing sequence numbers injects a forged packet with RST flag set and spoofed source IP/port matching the victim's connection

identifies requirement: injected RST sequence number must fall within the receiver's current receive window (`rwnd`) to be accepted (RFC 5961 adds challenge ACK checks to harden against RST injection)

questions.question: What is Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP, RFC 4960), and how do multi-homing and multi-streaming make it superior to TCP for telecom signaling (SS7/SIGTRAN)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Multi-Homing: a single SCTP association binds to multiple IP addresses on different network interfaces; automatically fails over to backup IP if primary link fails without terminating association
defines Multi-Streaming: multiplexes multiple independent message streams within one association, preventing head-of-line blocking between streams
defines Message-Oriented: preserves application message boundaries (like UDP) while ensuring reliable, sequenced delivery (like TCP)
explains 4-Way Handshake with Cookie Echo: server signs a state cookie during handshake to prevent SYN flood attacks, requiring zero server state allocation until the 4th message

questions.question: How does the TCP Urgent Pointer and URG flag operate, and why do modern application protocols avoid its use in favor of out-of-band application framing?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines URG flag: signals that the 16-bit Urgent Pointer field contains valid offset data pointing to the last byte of urgent/out-of-band data
explains original use case: Telnet or FTP command interrupts (e.g. sending Ctrl+C to abort a long running terminal command without waiting for buffered data to clear)

identifies historical RFC ambiguity: RFC 793 stated Urgent Pointer points to the byte AFTER urgent data, while BSD implementations made it point TO the last byte, creating persistent interoperability defects
notes modern avoidance: stream multiplexing (HTTP/2, WebSockets) and distinct application-level control channels replace legacy urgent pointers

questions.question: How does Receive Side Scaling (RSS) distribute incoming network packet processing across multiple CPU cores in high-throughput network interfaces?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies single-core bottleneck: on high-speed NICs (10G/40G/100G), a single CPU core handling all packet interrupts reaches 100% saturation while other cores remain idle
explains RSS mechanism: NIC hardware contains multiple independent Receive (Rx) descriptor queues mapped to distinct CPU cores via MSI-X interrupts
explains Toeplitz hashing: NIC hardware computes a hash of packet headers (4-tuple: IP/ports) and uses the lower bits to index an Indirection Table pointing to a CPU core
highlights cache locality: all packets belonging to the same TCP connection consistently hit the exact same CPU core, maximizing L1/L2 CPU cache hits and eliminating lock contention

questions.question: What is Generic Segmentation Offload (GSO) and TCP Segmentation Offload (TSO), and how do they reduce kernel CPU overhead when transmitting large bursts of data?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies traditional overhead: kernel TCP stack slices large application writes into 1460-byte MSS chunks, calculating IP/TCP headers and checksums for thousands of individual packets per second

explains TSO (Hardware Offload): kernel constructs a single massive buffer (up to 64KB `sk_buff`) with one set of headers and hands it directly to the NIC; NIC hardware breaks the buffer into MSS chunks and computes checksums at wire speed
explains GSO (Software Offload): if the NIC does not support TSO hardware, the kernel delays segmentation until the lowest driver layer right before transmitting to the wire
quantifies benefit: reduces system calls, memory traversals, and CPU utilization by up to 50-70% for heavy send operations

questions.question: What is Large Receive Offload (LRO) versus Generic Receive Offload (GRO) on packet ingress, and why is LRO unsafe on routing/forwarding appliances?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines LRO (Hardware Offload): NIC aggregates consecutive incoming TCP packets belonging to the same stream into a single massive super-packet before passing it up the kernel stack

explains why LRO is unsafe for routers/firewalls: LRO strips and discards individual IP/TCP headers during merging, making it impossible to forward original packet structures or preserve precise header fields
defines GRO (Generic Receive Offload): kernel software implementation that strictly validates and preserves original header metadata, making it safe for both end-hosts and forwarding bridges/routers
highlights performance: GRO cuts kernel per-packet processing overhead dramatically while maintaining protocol conformance

questions.question: What is the Nagle-delayed ACK deadlock problem, and what specific socket option and programming patterns eliminate it in client-server request-response protocols?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains root cause: client executes two small sequential `write()` calls (e.g. 100-byte header, then 200-byte body); client kernel sends first write and buffers second due to Nagle; server kernel delays ACK waiting for more data or timeout; 200ms latency stall occurs
remedy 1 (`TCP_NODELAY`): disables Nagle algorithm completely via `setsockopt(fd, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &val, sizeof(val))`
remedy 2 (`writev` / Scatter-Gather I/O): combine header and payload into an `iovec` array and transmit in a single atomic system call, ensuring a single combined packet is emitted
remedy 3 (`TCP_CORK` / `MSG_MORE`): explicitly instructs kernel to hold data until cork is removed, aggregating logical writes into a single full MSS segment before transmission

questions.question: How does TCP Pacing smooth out packet transmission to prevent packet bursts and microburst queue drops in datacenter switches?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains packet bursting: standard TCP sends a burst of packets equal to `cwnd` all at once upon receiving an ACK or after window inflation

explains microburst consequence: sudden bursts of 20-50 packets instantly overwhelm shallow switch buffers in low-latency datacenter switches, causing tail drops even when average link utilization is low
explains TCP Pacing mechanism: schedules packet transmissions evenly spaced across the Round-Trip Time (RTT) using high-resolution kernel timers (e.g. Linux `sch_fq`)
highlights integration: pacing is a foundational prerequisite for Google's BBR congestion control to accurately regulate delivery rate

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP Fast Open (TFO, RFC 7413) and standard TCP 3-way handshake, and how does the TFO Cookie protect against amplification attacks?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies limitation of standard TCP: client cannot include application data (HTTP GET) in the initial SYN packet; data transfer begins only on the 3rd packet (1 RTT delay)
explains TFO initial handshake: client requests a TFO cookie in the SYN; server generates an encrypted cookie and returns it in SYN-ACK

explains subsequent TFO connection: client sends SYN packet containing BOTH the TFO Cookie and early application data; server verifies cookie and delivers data to application immediately before 3-way handshake completes (saving 1 RTT)
explains cookie security: cookie proves client previously completed a 3-way handshake from that IP, preventing attackers from using forged SYN payloads for reflection/amplification attacks

questions.question: How does Data Center TCP (DCTCP, RFC 8257) achieve ultra-low latency and high throughput in private datacenter networks using multi-bit ECN feedback?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies standard ECN limitation: standard TCP treats ECN CE mark as a binary signal (halving cwnd whether 1 packet or 100 packets were marked)
explains DCTCP marking threshold: datacenter switches set ECN marks at very low queue thresholds (e.g. >10-20 packets) to detect early buffer buildup
explains fractional ECN feedback: receiver provides precise feedback on the EXACT fraction of bytes marked with ECN over the last RTT window

explains proportional window reduction: sender scales down its congestion window in direct proportion to the marked fraction (e.g. reduces cwnd by only 5% if 5% of packets were marked), maintaining high throughput with near-zero queue depths

questions.question: What is the function of the SO_REUSEPORT socket option in Linux, and how does kernel-level load balancing across multiple worker processes differ from SO_REUSEADDR?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines SO_REUSEADDR: allows binding to a port currently in TIME_WAIT state; does NOT allow multiple active processes to bind to the same IP:Port simultaneously
defines SO_REUSEPORT: allows multiple independent processes or threads to bind to the EXACT SAME port (provided all share the same effective user ID)
explains kernel distribution mechanism: kernel automatically load balances incoming SYN connections across the listening sockets using a 4-tuple hash
contrasts with single-socket worker models: eliminates the classical 'thundering herd' problem and epoll lock contention where multiple workers contend for a single shared listen socket

questions.question: How does Retransmission Timeout (RTO) calculation in RFC 6298 balance Smoothed RTT (SRTT) and RTT Variation (RTTVAR) to avoid spurious retransmissions?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains difference formula: upon measuring sample RTT `R`, computes difference `Err = R - SRTT`
updates variance: `RTTVAR = (1 - beta) * RTTVAR + beta * |Err|` (typically beta = 0.25)
updates smoothed RTT: `SRTT = (1 - alpha) * SRTT + alpha * R` (typically alpha = 0.125)
calculates RTO: `RTO = SRTT + max(G, K * RTTVAR)` where K=4; sets minimum floor (typically 1 second or 200ms) to prevent hair-trigger retransmissions on jittery links

questions.question: What is Path MTU Discovery failure due to ICMP filtering, and how does TCP MSS Clamping on border routers solve it without client-side reconfiguration?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains failure: sender sets DF=1; packet exceeds MTU on intermediate tunnel; router drops packet and sends ICMP Fragmentation Needed; security firewall blocks ICMP, leaving sender unaware
symptom: TCP connection handshakes succeed (small SYN packets pass), but bulk data transfers hang indefinitely
explains MSS Clamping solution: router at network edge inspects passing TCP SYN packets, checks interface MTU, and rewrites the MSS option header field downward to match link MTU minus 40 bytes
benefits: requires zero configuration changes on thousands of remote client workstations or mobile devices

questions.question: What is the TCP Window Probe timeout, and why does an unacknowledged Zero Window Probe cause a connection to terminate with ETIMEDOUT?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains persist timer: when rwnd drops to 0, sender starts a persist timer to periodically send 1-byte Zero Window Probes
explains backoff behavior: persist timer backs off exponentially (e.g. 1.5s, 3s, 6s... up to 60s cap)
describes failure condition: if receiver application completely deadlocks or crashes without sending a window update or responding to probes for `tcp_retries2` attempts
identifies outcome: sender kernel aborts the connection, deallocates socket buffers, and returns ETIMEDOUT to the writing process

questions.question: How does Forward RTO Recovery (F-RTO, RFC 5682) detect whether an RTO expiration was spurious (caused by sudden delay spike rather than packet loss)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies spurious RTO: on wireless/cellular links, handovers or radio re-transmissions cause temporary latency spikes exceeding RTO even though packets are not lost
explains F-RTO action upon RTO: retransmits only the FIRST unacknowledged segment and pauses sending further retransmissions
evaluates first ACK: when the first ACK arrives after timeout, sender transmits TWO BRAND NEW previously unsent packets

evaluates second ACK: if the second ACK acknowledges the newly sent packets (rather than duplicate ACKs), F-RTO proves the original packets were merely delayed; sender restores cwnd and ssthresh without retransmitting the remaining window

questions.question: What is the TCP Out-of-Order Queue (OFO Queue) in the Linux networking stack, and how does excessive memory consumption in the OFO queue trigger packet drops?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines OFO Queue: Red-Black tree inside kernel socket buffer holding out-of-order segments awaiting missing sequence gaps
identifies memory allocation: out-of-order packets consume real kernel memory (`sk_buff` structs and page allocations) accounted against `tcp_rmem` and global `tcp_mem`
explains kernel pruning: when socket memory exceeds limits, the kernel executes memory pruning (dropping segments from the OFO queue)
explains performance penalty: dropped out-of-order segments force the sender to retransmit data that was already successfully received, compounding network congestion

questions.question: How does TCP SYN Flood mitigation using SYN Proxy work on enterprise hardware firewalls without modifying the protected backend web servers?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains two-phase handshake: firewall intercepts SYN from client and replies directly with SYN-ACK (using SYN cookies) without forwarding to backend server
verifies client legitimacy: firewall waits for client's final ACK; if client never sends ACK (spoofed SYN flood), firewall drops half-open connection without backend server ever knowing
initiates backend connection: once client is verified, firewall completes a separate 3-way handshake with the backend server
explains sequence number splicing: firewall rewrites sequence and acknowledgment numbers on all subsequent packets to bridge the sequence number delta between client and backend connections

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP Reno, NewReno, and Tahoe in handling multiple packet drops in a single transmission window?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains TCP Tahoe: drops cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts Slow Start on ANY loss, handling multiple drops gracefully but with extreme throughput penalty
explains TCP Reno failure: Reno exits Fast Recovery on the very FIRST partial ACK, mistaking it for full recovery; subsequent dropped packets trigger an expensive RTO timeout and stall
explains TCP NewReno fix: introduces Partial ACK handling; stays in Fast Recovery upon receiving partial ACKs and immediately retransmits the next missing segment
concludes: NewReno avoids RTO timeouts during multiple packet drops within a single window without requiring SACK support

questions.question: How does UDP Multicast avoid packet replication on the sender by offloading replication to intermediate multicast-enabled routers?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies unicast replication overhead: sending video stream to 10,000 clients over unicast requires sender to generate 10,000 duplicate packets, saturating server NIC and uplink
explains multicast approach: sender transmits ONE single UDP packet addressed to a Class D multicast group (224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255)
explains router replication: intermediate routers examine their multicast routing tables (built via PIM/IGMP) and replicate the packet ONLY at branch points where receivers exist
notes bandwidth conservation: backbone links carry only a single copy of the stream regardless of the number of downstream viewers

questions.question: What is the Nagle algorithm implementation logic in pseudo-code, and under what two conditions does it permit packet transmission?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: states the condition: if there is new data to send, send immediately IF: (1) payload size >= MSS, OR (2) all previously transmitted data has been acknowledged (no unacknowledged data in flight)
states the buffering condition: otherwise (payload < MSS and unacknowledged data exists), buffer the data in the send queue until an ACK arrives or enough data accumulates to fill an MSS
explains self-clocking property: transmission rate automatically adjusts to network latency (on fast networks ACKs return quickly, releasing buffered packets rapidly)
explains why small interactive keystrokes are batched if the user types faster than round-trip network latency

questions.question: How does TCP SYN/ACK reflection attack turn open third-party servers into unwitting DDoS amplifiers against a victim IP?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains spoofing step: attacker sends SYN packets to thousands of legitimate Internet servers, spoofing the victim's IP as the packet source
explains reflection step: victim receives thousands of unexpected SYN-ACK replies from servers across the globe
explains amplification factor: when victim fails to respond, servers retransmit SYN-ACKs multiple times (exponential backoff over 30-60 seconds), multiplying the volume of unsolicited traffic
identifies defense: ingress/egress BCP 38 anti-spoofing filtering at ISP edges prevents attackers from injecting spoofed source IP packets

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP Keepalive and Application-Level Heartbeats (e.g. WebSocket Ping/Pong or HTTP/2 PING frames)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: compares layer: TCP keepalive runs strictly inside the OS kernel; application heartbeats run in user-space application code
identifies proxy blind spot: TCP keepalive operates hop-by-hop (only tests link between client and reverse proxy); if backend application crashes or threadpool deadlocks, TCP connection stays alive
highlights application heartbeat advantage: end-to-end verification; validates that the remote application event loop is actually responsive and processing messages
notes timing granularity: TCP keepalives default to hours (too slow for real-time failover), whereas application pings run every few seconds

questions.question: How does SO_LINGER socket option control socket close behavior, and what are the operational risks of setting l_onoff=1 with l_linger=0?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains default behavior (l_onoff=0): `close()` returns immediately, and kernel sends queued data in background followed by standard FIN teardown
explains positive linger (l_onoff=1, l_linger>0): `close()` blocks until all queued data is acknowledged by peer or timeout expires
explains zero linger (l_onoff=1, l_linger=0): kernel immediately aborts connection, flushes all unsent send buffer data, sends a TCP RST, and transitions directly to CLOSED (skipping TIME_WAIT)
identifies operational hazard: unread data in transit is discarded, remote peer receives Connection Reset error instead of clean EOF, and historical socket audits fail

questions.question: In Linux TCP tuning, what roles do 'tcp_wmem', 'tcp_rmem', and 'tcp_mem' play in regulating buffer allocation and preventing out-of-memory kernel panics?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains `tcp_rmem` / `tcp_wmem`: vector of 3 integers (min, default, max) specifying receive and send buffer memory in BYTES per socket
explains autotuning: kernel dynamically scales socket buffers between min and max based on measured Bandwidth-Delay Product
defines `tcp_mem`: vector of 3 integers (min, pressure, max) measuring GLOBAL TCP memory across all sockets in 4KB PAGES (not bytes)
explains memory pressure thresholds: above 'pressure', kernel throttles buffer sizes and enters memory pressure mode; above 'max', kernel begins dropping incoming packets to prevent system OOM panic

questions.question: What is the complete end-to-end resolution workflow when a client queries an uncached domain name, traversing Root, TLD, and Authoritative DNS servers?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: distinguishes queries: Client sends a RECURSIVE query to local ISP/public resolver (e.g. 8.8.8.8); resolver performs ITERATIVE queries upstream
step 1: Resolver queries a Root Name Server (one of 13 root IP identities); Root responds with a referral to the TLD nameserver (e.g. .com TLD)
step 2: Resolver queries the TLD nameserver; TLD responds with a referral to the authoritative nameserver for that specific domain (along with glue records)
step 3: Resolver queries the Authoritative nameserver, which returns the final Resource Record (A/AAAA) and TTL, which the resolver caches and returns to the client

questions.question: What are DNS Glue Records, and why are they required when a domain's authoritative nameserver is hosted within its own domain zone (e.g. ns1.example.com for example.com)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines the circular dependency problem: to resolve `example.com`, resolver must query its nameserver `ns1.example.com`; but resolving `ns1.example.com` requires querying `example.com`, creating an infinite resolution loop
defines Glue Record: an 'A' or 'AAAA' record providing the literal IP address of the nameserver embedded directly inside the parent zone (e.g. the `.com` TLD registry)
explains resolution: when the TLD nameserver delegates `example.com` to `ns1.example.com`, it includes the glue IP in the 'Additional Records' section of the DNS referral
identifies consequences of missing glue: resolution fails completely with circular referral errors across all recursive resolvers

questions.question: What is the difference between DNS CNAME, ALIAS (ANAME), and A records, and why does RFC 1034 forbid placing a CNAME at the zone apex (@ / root domain)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines CNAME: maps an alias hostname to another canonical domain name (e.g. `www.example.com` -> `cdn.provider.net`)
explains RFC 1034 rule: if a CNAME record exists for a node name, NO other record types (MX, TXT, NS, SOA) may exist for that same name
explains zone apex failure: the zone apex (`example.com`) MUST contain mandatory SOA and NS records; adding a CNAME at the apex violates RFC 1034 and breaks email/nameserver resolution
defines ALIAS / ANAME solution: proprietary DNS provider records that dynamically resolve the target CNAME to an IP address at query time and return a standard 'A' record at the apex

questions.question: How did the Dan Kaminsky DNS Cache Poisoning attack bypass transaction ID randomization, and how did Source Port Randomization (RFC 5452) mitigate it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies traditional limit: guessing the 16-bit Transaction ID (65,536 possibilities) for an existing domain gave attackers only 1 chance before the legitimate reply arrived and was cached

explains Kaminsky innovation: attacker queries random non-existent subdomains (`random123.example.com`), forcing the target resolver to query the authoritative server repeatedly without waiting for cache timeouts
explains injection mechanism: attacker floods thousands of spoofed replies containing forged authoritative 'NS' records claiming `attacker.com` is authoritative for the entire `example.com` zone

explains mitigation: Source Port Randomization adds 16 bits of UDP source port entropy to the 16-bit transaction ID, expanding search space to 2^32 (~4.3 billion combinations), rendering brute-force poisoning computationally infeasible

questions.question: How does DNSSEC establish cryptographic integrity and authentication of DNS records through RRSIG, DNSKEY, and DS records forming a chain of trust to the Root zone?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains RRSIG: every resource record set (RRset) is digitally signed with a cryptographic signature stored in an RRSIG record
distinguishes ZSK and KSK: Zone Signing Key (ZSK) signs daily resource records; Key Signing Key (KSK) signs the ZSK to validate zone keys
explains Delegation Signer (DS): parent zone stores a cryptographic hash of the child zone's KSK in a DS record, binding parent and child
traces Chain of Trust: validating resolver verifies signatures iteratively up the tree until reaching the internationally trusted, hardcoded DNSSEC Root KSK

questions.question: What are the privacy differences between DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484) and DNS-over-TLS (DoT, RFC 7858), and why does DoH spark debate regarding network perimeter visibility?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines DoT: encrypts standard DNS queries inside TLS over a dedicated port (TCP port 853); easy for enterprise firewalls to monitor or block
defines DoH: wraps DNS queries inside HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 HTTPS POST/GET requests over standard TCP port 443
highlights DoH invisibility: because DoH shares port 443 with all web browsing traffic, network eavesdroppers and ISPs cannot distinguish DNS lookups from regular website traffic
identifies enterprise controversy: DoH bypasses corporate DNS monitoring, parental controls, and enterprise malware filtering unless enterprise roots are injected to decrypt TLS

questions.question: How does a DNS Amplification DDoS attack exploit open recursive resolvers and EDNS0 to achieve massive 50x to 100x traffic amplification factors?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains spoofed reflection: attacker sends small UDP DNS query packets (approx 60 bytes) to open recursive DNS resolvers across the Internet, spoofing the victim's IP as the source
explains EDNS0 extension: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS0, RFC 6891) advertises client buffer sizes up to 4096 bytes (overcoming legacy 512-byte UDP limits)
explains amplification: querying for 'ANY' records on heavily configured DNSSEC-signed domains returns massive cryptographic keys and signatures (3000-4000 bytes)
calculates amplification factor: a 60-byte request generating a 3600-byte response achieves a 60x traffic multiplication, overwhelming victim uplinks with gigabits of reflected traffic

questions.question: What is the mandatory role of the 'Host' header in HTTP/1.1, and how does it enable Virtual Hosting of multiple distinct domains on a single shared IP address?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains the HTTP/1.0 limitation: requests contained only URI paths (e.g. `GET /index.html`); if multiple domain names resolved to the same IP, the web server had no way to determine which site was requested
explains HTTP/1.1 requirement: RFC 2616 made the `Host: <hostname>` header strictly mandatory on all requests (returning 400 Bad Request if missing)
explains virtual hosting: the web server (e.g. Nginx, Apache) inspects the `Host` header to route the request to the matching server block / virtual host directory
notes conservation: allows hosting hundreds of independent websites and customer domains on a single public IPv4 address

questions.question: How does HTTP/1.1 Chunked Transfer Encoding (Transfer-Encoding: chunked) allow streaming responses of dynamically generated content whose total length is unknown in advance?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies the problem: persistent HTTP/1.1 connections require knowing when a response ends; statically buffering a dynamic 10GB database export to calculate `Content-Length` exhausts server RAM and adds massive delay

explains chunk framing format: server sends data in sequential chunks, each formatted as: `<hexadecimal byte count>
<raw data>
`

explains stream termination: a zero-sized chunk (`0

`) signals the definitive end of the HTTP message body
identifies chunk trailers: allows sending trailing metadata (such as SHA-256 checksums calculated on-the-fly) after the payload stream completes

questions.question: What is the Binary Framing Layer in HTTP/2 (RFC 7540), and what are the core frame types (DATA, HEADERS, SETTINGS, RST_STREAM, GOAWAY)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains architectural shift: replaces HTTP/1.1 plaintext newline-delimited ASCII text with an efficient 9-byte binary frame header (Length, Type, Flags, Stream ID)
defines HEADERS frame: carries HTTP request/response headers compressed with HPACK
defines DATA frame: carries raw message payload data for a specific Stream ID
defines RST_STREAM: allows client or server to immediately cancel an individual stream without closing the underlying TCP connection
defines GOAWAY: graceful connection shutdown announcing the highest Stream ID processed, allowing pending streams to finish

questions.question: How does HPACK (RFC 7541) compress HTTP/2 headers using a Static Table, Dynamic Table, and Huffman Coding, and why does it avoid CRIME and BREACH compression attacks?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Static Table: predefined index of 61 common HTTP headers (e.g. index 2 = `GET`, index 7 = `:scheme: https`) requiring only a single byte to transmit

explains Dynamic Table: stateful table maintained independently on both endpoints that caches custom header fields across requests, transmitting subsequent identical headers as simple index references
explains Static Huffman Coding: compresses variable string literals using a pre-computed Huffman codebook tailored to HTTP header frequencies

explains CRIME attack mitigation: standard gzip/DEFLATE compresses repeated strings across headers and cookies, allowing attackers to sniff secrets by observing ciphertext length; HPACK isolates header keys and uses static Huffman trees to prevent length-leakage side-channel attacks

questions.question: What is HTTP/2 Server Push, why did it fail to achieve widespread production adoption, and why was it removed from Google Chrome?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Server Push mechanism: server anticipates client needs (e.g. pushing `style.css` when `index.html` is requested) by sending a `PUSH_PROMISE` frame before the client asks

identifies Cache Blindness failure: server has no visibility into the browser's local cache; server frequently pushes megabytes of CSS/JS assets that the browser already cached locally, wasting mobile bandwidth
identifies Racing and Contention: pushed resources compete for bandwidth with critical in-flight rendering assets, often delaying page First Contentful Paint (FCP)
explains modern replacement: HTTP status code `103 Early Hints` with `Link: rel=preload` headers, allowing the browser to check its own cache before fetching

questions.question: How does QPACK (RFC 9204) adapt header compression for HTTP/3 over QUIC without causing Head-of-Line blocking between independent streams?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies HPACK limitation: HPACK requires strict in-order delivery of all headers across all streams; in HTTP/3, QUIC delivers streams out of order, which would re-introduce head-of-line blocking if HPACK were used
explains QPACK architecture: separates header compression state from individual request streams using dedicated unidirectional Encoder and Decoder control streams
explains dynamic table synchronization: instructions modifying the dynamic table are sent over the encoder stream, while acknowledgments return over the decoder stream
explains non-blocking references: streams can reference dynamic entries without stalling unless an unacknowledged entry is strictly required, preserving full out-of-order stream processing

questions.question: How does the WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) establish a persistent full-duplex connection via the HTTP Upgrade handshake, and what is the role of Sec-WebSocket-Key?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains handshake request: client sends HTTP GET with headers `Connection: Upgrade`, `Upgrade: websocket`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`, and a random base64-encoded `Sec-WebSocket-Key`

explains server response: server responds with `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`, computing `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` by taking the client key, concatenating a globally unique GUID (`258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`), taking the SHA-1 hash, and base64-encoding the result
explains verification: proves server understands WebSocket protocol and is not an accidental HTTP reverse proxy cache
explains socket transition: the underlying TCP connection remains open, switching immediately from HTTP text to lightweight bidirectional binary WebSocket frames

questions.question: Why does the WebSocket protocol strictly require 4-byte client-to-server Frame Masking, and what proxy cache poisoning attack does it prevent?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains masking mechanism: client generates a cryptographically random 4-byte masking key for every single frame and XORs all payload bytes with this key before transmitting; server unmasks with the same key

identifies the attack without masking: an attacker script running in a victim's browser could send a WebSocket payload crafted to look exactly like an HTTP GET request (e.g. `GET /script.js HTTP/1.1`)
explains proxy confusion: a transparent corporate proxy or gateway mistaking the connection for HTTP could cache the malicious payload as a response to legitimate requests (proxy cache poisoning)
concludes: XOR masking with random keys ensures that the wire representation is randomized and unpredictable, preventing intermediaries from misinterpreting payloads as plaintext HTTP

questions.question: How do Server-Sent Events (SSE) compare to WebSockets in terms of transport protocol, directionality, reconnection handling, and HTTP/2 multiplexing compatibility?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: compares directionality: WebSockets provide bidirectional full-duplex communication; SSE is strictly unidirectional (server pushing events to client)
compares protocol: WebSockets switch protocol away from HTTP; SSE is standard HTTP (`Content-Type: text/event-stream`), traversing all standard proxies and firewalls without special configuration

explains reconnection: SSE includes built-in browser client reconnection and event ID tracking (`Last-Event-ID` header) to resume dropped streams without data loss; WebSockets require custom application code
highlights HTTP/2 synergy: SSE multiplexes natively over HTTP/2 connections alongside regular assets, whereas WebSockets historically bypassed HTTP/2 multiplexing

questions.question: What is the difference between Strong Validators (ETag) and Weak Validators (Last-Modified / W/"...") in HTTP conditional caching?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Strong Validator (e.g. `ETag: "abc123"`): guarantees exact byte-for-byte identity of the representation; mandatory for byte-range requests (`Range: bytes=...`)

defines Weak Validator (e.g. `ETag: W/"abc123"` or `Last-Modified`): indicates semantic equivalence; content is functionally identical (e.g. same HTML content but updated timestamp or compressed differently)
explains conditional request: client sends cached validator in `If-None-Match: "abc123"` or `If-Modified-Since`; server responds with `304 Not Modified` without payload if unchanged
identifies limitation of `Last-Modified`: has 1-second resolution (unable to capture sub-second file changes) and clock skews between servers corrupt validation

questions.question: How do 'Cache-Control: no-cache', 'no-store', 'public', 'private', and 'stale-while-revalidate' directives govern browser and intermediary caching behavior?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: distinguishes `no-cache` vs `no-store`: `no-cache` caches the response but mandates revalidation with origin server (using ETag) before serving; `no-store` forbids any caching in disk or memory (for sensitive financial data)
distinguishes `public` vs `private`: `private` restricts caching strictly to the end-user's browser (forbidden on shared CDN/proxies); `public` permits caching by any intermediary
explains `stale-while-revalidate`: instructs client to serve the cached (stale) version immediately for zero-latency rendering while triggering an asynchronous background fetch to refresh the cache
explains `max-age` and `s-maxage`: `max-age` defines freshness TTL in seconds for browser; `s-maxage` overrides TTL specifically for shared CDN caches

questions.question: What is the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) preflight request, and what exact criteria trigger an OPTIONS preflight exchange?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Simple Request: uses GET, HEAD, or POST; allowed headers are strictly Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type; Content-Type is limited to `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, or `text/plain`
identifies preflight triggers: any other HTTP method (PUT, DELETE, PATCH) OR custom headers (e.g. `Authorization`, `X-Custom-Header`) OR `Content-Type: application/json`
explains OPTIONS preflight: browser sends OPTIONS request with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method`, and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`
explains server grant: server replies with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`; only upon approval does browser issue actual request

questions.question: Why does CORS allow credentials (cookies, HTTP authentication) only if 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true' is present, and why is a wildcard '*' forbidden for the origin in this mode?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains credentialed request: when a cross-origin fetch sets `credentials: 'include'`, the browser attaches cookies and authorization headers to the request
explains server requirement: server must explicitly respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` AND reflect the EXACT matching requesting origin in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`

explains why wildcard `*` is prohibited: allowing `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials would permit ANY malicious website on the Internet to read authenticated session data and private user profiles from any intranet service
explains browser enforcement: if server returns wildcard `*` with credentials true, browser automatically rejects the response and throws a CORS security exception

questions.question: What is the complete 1-RTT handshake sequence of TLS 1.3, and how does it achieve lower latency and higher security compared to TLS 1.2?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: traces 1-RTT flow: Client sends `ClientHello` guessing supported cipher and speculative `KeyShare` (ECDHE public key); Server responds with `ServerHello` + `KeyShare` + `EncryptedExtensions` + `Certificate` + `Finished` in a single round-trip
explains latency reduction: drops full handshake from 2 RTTs in TLS 1.2 down to 1 RTT in TLS 1.3
explains security hardening: mandates Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE), guaranteeing Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS); completely removes static RSA key exchange
removes legacy vulnerabilities: eliminates vulnerable ciphers (RC4, 3DES, CBC mode ciphers prone to Lucky Thirteen/POODLE, MD5, SHA-1)

questions.question: What is Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), and how does Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) protect past encrypted communications if a server's private key is compromised in the future?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies static RSA flaw: client encrypts pre-master secret with server's static public key; an adversary who records encrypted Internet traffic can decrypt ALL historical recorded sessions if the server's private key is stolen years later
explains PFS definition: compromise of a long-term private key does NOT compromise the confidentiality of past session keys
explains ECDHE mechanism: endpoints generate unique, temporary (ephemeral) public/private key pairs for every single session, computing the shared secret independently
explains ephemeral destruction: endpoints securely erase ephemeral private keys from memory immediately after deriving session keys, making retrospective decryption mathematically impossible

questions.question: How does Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) validate an X.509 server certificate through a hierarchical Chain of Trust up to a trusted Root CA?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains certificate components: public key, Subject (domain name), Issuer, Validity period, and CA Digital Signature
explains Intermediate CA role: Root CAs stay offline in secure air-gapped vaults; Root CA signs Intermediate CA certificates, which issue end-entity server certificates
explains verification chain: client verifies leaf certificate using Intermediate CA's public key; verifies Intermediate CA using Root CA's public key
explains trust anchor: Root CA is self-signed and pre-installed in the operating system / browser trusted root certificate store

questions.question: What is the difference between Certificate Revocation Lists (CRL), Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), and OCSP Stapling (RFC 6066)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines CRL: client downloads periodic massive list of revoked certificate serial numbers; high bandwidth overhead and stale updates
defines OCSP: client queries CA's OCSP responder in real-time for single certificate status; causes latency on every connection and leaks client browsing history to CA (privacy issue)
defines OCSP Stapling: server queries CA's OCSP responder periodically, caches the signed status response, and 'staples' it directly into the TLS handshake (CertificateStatus message)
identifies benefits of stapling: eliminates client lookup latency, protects client privacy, and prevents denial of service from CA downtime

questions.question: What is Server Name Indication (SNI) in TLS, and why does Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) protect privacy against ISP traffic eavesdropping?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains SNI necessity: during initial TLS handshake, client must tell the server which hostname it wants so the server presents the correct SSL certificate before decryption occurs

identifies SNI privacy flaw: SNI in standard TLS 1.3 is transmitted in CLEARTEXT inside ClientHello, allowing ISPs, governments, and network sniffers to track visited domain names despite HTTPS encryption
explains ECH mechanism: client fetches server's public key via DNS (HTTPS record) and encrypts the real `ClientHelloInner` containing the target hostname inside an outer dummy `ClientHelloOuter`
highlights privacy benefit: network eavesdroppers see only the shared CDN fronting domain, fully concealing the specific visited website

questions.question: How does HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) prevent SSL Stripping attacks, and what is the HSTS Preload List?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains SSL Stripping (Moxie Marlinspike): attacker intercepts initial plaintext HTTP request and strips 301/302 redirects to HTTPS, proxying victim over cleartext HTTP while attacker talks HTTPS to server
explains HSTS header: server sends `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload`, instructing browser to NEVER send cleartext HTTP to this domain
explains client-side enforcement: browser automatically rewrites all `http://` links to `https://` internally before sending packets and strictly refuses to bypass certificate errors
explains HSTS Preload: hardcodes domains directly into browser binary source code, protecting users even on their very first connection attempt (Trust-On-First-Use gap)

questions.question: What is BGP Prefix Hijacking, why does the Longest Prefix Match rule make sub-prefix hijacking devastating, and how does RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) mitigate it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains BGP trust model: standard BGP has zero built-in authentication; routers blindly trust and propagate route advertisements from peers

explains Sub-Prefix Hijacking: if legitimate owner advertises `203.0.113.0/24`, an attacker advertises more specific `/25` subnets; all Internet routers prefer the `/25` route due to Longest Prefix Match, redirecting global traffic to attacker
explains RPKI: uses cryptographic certificates to bind IP address blocks to authorized Autonomous System Numbers (ASN) in Route Origin Authorization (ROA) records
explains Route Origin Validation (ROV): border routers drop BGP updates that are cryptographically invalid, preventing hijacked routes from propagating

questions.question: How does a Slowloris DDoS attack incapacitate thread-per-connection web servers (like Apache) using minimal bandwidth, and why are event-driven servers (like Nginx) immune?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria:
explains attack mechanism: attacker opens hundreds of HTTP connections and sends incomplete headers very slowly (e.g. sending one header line every 15 seconds: `X-a: b
`), never sending the terminating `

`
explains thread exhaustion (Apache): thread-per-connection servers allocate an entire worker thread/process to each open socket; threads block waiting for headers until threadpool is 100% exhausted
explains event-driven immunity (Nginx): uses asynchronous non-blocking event loops (`epoll`/`kqueue`); thousands of idle connections consume only minimal memory without blocking worker processes
proposes defenses: enforce strict client header timeouts (`client_header_timeout`), minimum data transfer rates, and reverse proxy buffering

questions.question: What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer (Layer 7) and a Network Load Balancer (Layer 4) in terms of connection termination, routing capabilities, and latency?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Layer 4 (NLB): operates on IP and TCP/UDP ports; forwards raw packets without terminating TCP; supports Direct Server Return (DSR); achieves millions of packets/sec with sub-millisecond latency
defines Layer 7 (ALB): terminates incoming TCP connections, decrypts TLS, parses HTTP headers, cookies, and URI paths before creating a separate backend connection
explains routing capability: Layer 7 enables smart routing (path-based routing, header rewriting, cookie sticky sessions, rate limiting); Layer 4 cannot inspect application payloads
highlights trade-off: Layer 7 adds latency and CPU load due to full TLS termination and buffering, whereas Layer 4 offers extreme wire-speed throughput

questions.question: How does Direct Server Return (DSR) in Layer 4 load balancing eliminate load balancer egress bottlenecks by allowing backend servers to reply directly to clients?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies traffic asymmetry: inbound requests are tiny (HTTP GET ~1KB), but outbound responses are massive (HTML/images/video megabytes), making load balancer egress uplink the primary bottleneck
explains DSR packet flow: load balancer rewrites destination MAC address to chosen backend server (or uses IP-in-IP tunnel) without modifying destination IP (keeps VIP intact)
explains server configuration: backend server configures the Virtual IP (VIP) on a non-ARPing loopback interface (`lo:0`) to accept packets addressed to VIP
explains direct reply: backend server generates response packet with Source IP = VIP and routes directly out its own gateway to the client, entirely bypassing the load balancer on egress

questions.question: How does Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) allocate IP addresses using the DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) process, and what is a DHCP Relay Agent?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: traces DORA steps: Discover (client broadcast on 255.255.255.255), Offer (server unicast/broadcast with IP lease), Request (client requests offered IP), Acknowledge (server commits lease)
identifies transport ports: UDP port 67 (server) and UDP port 68 (client)
identifies broadcast boundary: routers do not forward Layer 2 broadcast packets across subnets, meaning DHCP Discover cannot reach a centralized DHCP server on another network
explains DHCP Relay Agent (IP Helper): router intercepts client broadcast, converts it to unicast addressed to the central DHCP server, and relays the reply back to the local LAN

questions.question: What is Network Time Protocol (NTP, RFC 5905), how does the Stratum hierarchy organize time servers, and how does NTP filter network jitter using Marzullo's algorithm?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Stratum hierarchy: Stratum 0 (atomic clocks, GPS receivers); Stratum 1 (servers directly attached to Stratum 0); Stratum 2 (servers synchronized to Stratum 1 over network)
explains offset and delay calculation: records 4 timestamps: T1 (client send), T2 (server receive), T3 (server transmit), T4 (client receive)
states formulas: `Delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2)` and `Clock Offset = ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2`
explains clock discipline: slews local system clock gradually to prevent time jumps that would corrupt database transactions

questions.question: What is Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMPv3), and how does its User-based Security Model (USM) overcome the plaintext community string vulnerabilities of SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies SNMPv1/v2c weakness: uses plaintext 'Community Strings' (e.g. 'public' or 'private') transmitted unencrypted across the wire, susceptible to packet sniffing and unauthorized configuration modifications
explains SNMPv3 USM levels: `noAuthNoPriv` (username only, unencrypted), `authNoPriv` (authentication via HMAC-SHA/MD5, no encryption), and `authPriv` (authentication plus AES encryption)
explains View-based Access Control (VACM): restricts specific users to read/write access on granular subtrees of the Management Information Base (MIB)
notes operational role: allows network monitoring systems to securely query router interface metrics and receive asynchronous alerts (SNMP Traps on UDP port 162)

questions.question: How does Anycast DNS combined with GeoDNS optimize global content distribution by balancing latency, server capacity, and geographical traffic steering?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines Anycast DNS: BGP routes client to topologically nearest nameserver based on Internet routing hops, providing automatic DDoS absorption and resilience
defines GeoDNS: authoritative server inspects client IP (or EDNS Client Subnet, ECS) to return the IP address of the closest CDN edge server
compares layers: Anycast operates at Layer 3 (network routing); GeoDNS operates at Layer 7 (application DNS payload resolution)
explains hybrid synergy: Anycast routes user to the closest DNS resolver PoP, and GeoDNS returns the optimal regional application server, accounting for regional load and server health

questions.question: What is Origin Shielding in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs), and how does it prevent the 'thundering herd' cache miss storm from crashing origin backend databases?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies problem without shielding: a global CDN has hundreds of edge PoPs; when a popular asset expires or cache is purged, hundreds of PoPs query the origin simultaneously (cache stampede / thundering herd)
defines Origin Shield: a centralized intermediate caching layer situated between global edge PoPs and the origin backend infrastructure
explains request flow: edge PoPs on cache miss query the Origin Shield; only if the Shield misses does a single request reach the origin
explains Request Collapsing (Coalescing): consolidates concurrent duplicate requests for the same URI into a single backend fetch, boosting origin offload to >99%

questions.question: How does Session Resumption in TLS 1.3 using Pre-Shared Keys (PSK) differ from legacy TLS 1.2 Session Tickets (RFC 5077)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains TLS 1.2 Session Tickets: server encrypts session state with a secret Server Ticket Encryption Key (STEK) and sends it to client; client echoes ticket in ClientHello to resume
identifies TLS 1.2 vulnerability: if the STEK is compromised or not rotated frequently, forward secrecy of all resumed sessions is broken
explains TLS 1.3 unification: unifies session resumption and pre-shared keys into a single PSK mechanism via `NewSessionTicket` messages
highlights TLS 1.3 forward secrecy option: supports combining PSK resumption with an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key share (PSK-with-DHE), preserving Perfect Forward Secrecy even for resumed connections

questions.question: What is the structure of an SSH (Secure Shell) connection handshake, and how does it authenticate the host server while preventing Man-in-the-Middle attacks?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains protocol steps: version exchange (`SSH-2.0`), algorithm negotiation, Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish shared symmetric encryption and integrity keys
explains Host Authentication: server signs the Diffie-Hellman exchange hash using its permanent private host key; client verifies signature using server's public host key
explains Trust On First Use (TOFU): on first connection, client prompts user to accept public key fingerprint and stores it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`
explains MitM detection: on subsequent connections, if the host key changes, SSH aborts immediately with a high-severity warning, preventing active traffic interception

questions.question: What is gRPC, and why does its use of Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) over HTTP/2 provide significant performance gains compared to REST over JSON/HTTP/1.1?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: compares serialization: Protobuf is a compact binary format with field tags and varints, parsing 5x to 10x faster with smaller payload sizes than verbose text-based JSON
compares transport: REST over HTTP/1.1 suffers from connection overhead and head-of-line blocking; gRPC uses HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming multiple concurrent RPC calls over one TCP connection
identifies streaming capabilities: supports 4 interaction models: Unary, Server Streaming, Client Streaming, and Bidirectional Streaming
notes strongly-typed contracts: `.proto` IDL files auto-generate client stubs and server boilerplate across multiple programming languages

questions.question: How does BGP Anycast DDoS mitigation absorb volumetric multi-terabit attacks by scrubbing malicious traffic across distributed edge scrubbing centers?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains Anycast routing dilution: attack traffic originating from global botnets is naturally split across dozens of regional edge scrubbing data centers rather than converging on a single target datacenter
explains Scrubbing Center operation: specialized DDoS mitigation appliances filter out attack traffic (SYN floods, UDP amplification, DNS floods) using DPI and behavioral heuristics
explains Clean Traffic return: legitimate user traffic is encapsulated (via GRE or MPLS) and forwarded to the customer's actual origin servers
quantifies benefit: transforms a catastrophic 2 Tbps attack into manageable 20 Gbps chunks distributed across 100 global PoPs

questions.question: What is Network Address Translation Hairpinning (NAT Loopback), and why does a client on a private LAN fail to reach a local server using its public domain name without it?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: describes the scenario: internal host A (192.168.1.50) queries public DNS for `server.example.com`, receiving public WAN IP (203.0.113.1) mapped to internal server B (192.168.1.100)
identifies failure without hairpinning: router receives packet on LAN interface with destination IP = public WAN IP; standard routers drop the packet or route out WAN interface

explains asymmetric return problem: even if router translates destination to B, B sees source IP A (local subnet) and replies directly via Layer 2 switch; A drops reply because it expected response from 203.0.113.1

explains Hairpinning solution: router performs BOTH DNAT (destination to 192.168.1.100) AND SNAT (source to router IP 192.168.1.1), forcing server B to route return packets back through router to un-NAT properly

questions.question: How does Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) NSEC and NSEC3 prevent zone walking while proving the non-existence of a queried domain name (Authenticated Denial of Existence)?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies problem: an authoritative server cannot digitally sign non-existent domains in real time without holding private keys online

explains NSEC solution: lists existing domain names in sorted alphabetical order; to prove `b.example.com` does not exist, server returns a signed NSEC record showing the gap between `a.example.com` and `c.example.com`
identifies NSEC flaw (Zone Walking): an attacker querying gaps iteratively can dump the entire list of internal subdomains and hostnames in the zone
explains NSEC3 solution: replaces plaintext domain names with salted cryptographic hashes (e.g. gap between hash(a) and hash(c)), proving non-existence while preventing zone enumeration

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP SYN Cookie and SYN Cache implementations in operating system kernels under SYN flood conditions?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines SYN Cache: allocates a lightweight hash table entry (typically 160 bytes) storing connection metadata instead of allocating a full Transmission Control Block (TCB, ~1KB); drops oldest entries if flooded
defines SYN Cookies: allocates ZERO memory; encodes state into the 32-bit ISN returned in SYN-ACK
identifies SYN Cookie drawback: encoding limitations force dropping or quantizing TCP options (Window Scaling, SACK, Timestamps) unless encoded into timestamp bits
explains modern hybrid approach: kernels use SYN Cache under moderate load to preserve all TCP options, transitioning to stateless SYN Cookies only when SYN queue capacity is completely saturated

questions.question: How does Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP, RFC 5321) deliver email across mail transfer agents, and what are the security roles of SPF, DKIM, and DMARC?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains SMTP delivery: client/MTA uses DNS MX records to resolve recipient mail server, establishing TCP port 25 session using commands (HELO/EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA)
explains SPF (Sender Policy Framework): DNS TXT record specifying authorized sending IP addresses for the sender domain
explains DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): sender MTA signs email header/body with private key; recipient verifies signature using sender's public key published in DNS
explains DMARC: policy framework linking SPF and DKIM; instructs recipient MTAs how to handle failures (none, quarantine, reject) and provides reporting back to domain owners

questions.question: What is the Difference between HTTP/1.1 Pipelining and HTTP/2 Multiplexing in browser network resource fetching?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines HTTP/1.1 Pipelining: allows sending multiple requests over a single TCP connection without waiting for responses, BUT server is strictly mandated to return responses in the exact FIFO order requests were received

explains Pipelining failure: if Request 1 takes 5 seconds (heavy DB query), Responses 2 and 3 are blocked behind it (application Head-of-Line blocking); buggy proxies made pipelining disabled by default in all browsers
defines HTTP/2 Multiplexing: splits requests/responses into independent binary frames tagged with Stream IDs
highlights the advantage: frames from different streams are interleaved arbitrarily on the wire; slow responses do not delay fast responses

questions.question: How does Content-Security-Policy (CSP) HTTP response header mitigate Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and data exfiltration in web applications?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines CSP: HTTP header that restricts the resources (scripts, images, stylesheets, iframes) browser is allowed to load and execute for a given page
explains inline script restriction: forbids execution of unsafe inline scripts (`eval()`, inline `<script>` tags, inline event handlers) by default
explains Nonce-based CSP: server generates a cryptographically random single-use token per HTTP response (`script-src 'nonce-rAnd0m'`); only scripts containing matching nonce attribute are executed
explains exfiltration blocking: `connect-src` restricts destinations where `fetch()`, `XHR`, and WebSockets can transmit stolen data

questions.question: What is Certificate Transparency (CT, RFC 6962), and how do append-only public Merkle Trees prevent rogue Certificate Authorities from silently issuing fraudulent SSL certificates?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies PKI flaw: any compromised public CA (e.g. DigiNotar breach) can issue valid certificates for `google.com` to spy on users without the domain owner's knowledge
explains CT requirement: CAs must submit all newly issued certificates to public, append-only, cryptographically auditable Merkle Tree logs
explains Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT): log returns an SCT proof; web servers must include valid SCTs in TLS handshake (or embedded in certificate)
explains domain owner monitoring: domain owners monitor CT logs in real-time, receiving alerts within minutes if an unauthorized certificate is issued for their domain

questions.question: How does the BGP MED (Multi-Exit Discriminator) attribute control incoming traffic across multiple peering links with a neighboring Autonomous System, and why is MED comparison non-transitive?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: explains MED purpose: advertised to an external neighboring AS to convey which specific ingress link into the local AS is preferred for a destination prefix (lower MED is preferred)
explains non-transitive nature: MED is passed to the immediate neighboring AS, but that neighboring AS is strictly forbidden from propagating the MED value to third-party downstream ASes
explains comparison rule: by default, routers compare MED ONLY among paths received from the EXACT SAME neighboring Autonomous System
identifies path oscillation: receiving paths from different ASes can cause routing loops unless `bgp deterministic-med` or `always-compare-med` is enabled

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP Incast and TCP Outcast problems in high-density datacenter switch fabrics?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: defines TCP Incast: many synchronized servers concurrently reply to a single aggregator node (e.g. in MapReduce / distributed search); hundreds of simultaneous packet bursts overwhelm the shallow buffer of the egress switch port, causing heavy packet drops and RTO timeouts

defines TCP Outcast: severe throughput starvation that occurs when a high-bandwidth elephant flow and multiple low-bandwidth mice flows arrive on different switch ingress ports and contend for the same egress port
explains Outcast mechanism: switch tail-drop policies disproportionately drop packets from the port with fewer arriving packets, starving the low-bandwidth flows completely
proposes mitigations: low switch marking thresholds with DCTCP, deep shared-buffer switches, and microsecond RTO timers

questions.question: How does Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) combined with Forward Error Correction (Hybrid ARQ / HARQ) optimize cellular radio links in LTE and 5G?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: identifies trade-off: pure ARQ suffers high retransmission latency over radio; pure FEC wastes spectrum transmitting redundant parity bits on clean channels
explains HARQ: physical layer detects corrupted transport blocks and requests rapid hardware retransmissions (sub-millisecond) before Layer 2 RLC kicks in
explains Type I (Chase Combining): receiver buffers the corrupted packet; sender retransmits identical packet; receiver combines energy of both transmissions to boost SNR before decoding

explains Type II (Incremental Redundancy): sender retransmits additional parity bits rather than repeating data; receiver appends new parity to previous transmission for higher error-correction capability

questions.question: In enterprise network design, how do Zero Trust Network Architecture (ZTNA) principles replace traditional perimeter-based VPN security models?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
criteria: critiques traditional perimeter model ('Castle-and-Moat'): assumes all devices inside corporate LAN/VPN are trusted; once an attacker breaches VPN, they move laterally unchecked across internal subnets
states core Zero Trust axiom: 'Never Trust, Always Verify'; treats internal network as equally hostile as the public Internet
explains micro-segmentation and least privilege: access is granted per-application rather than per-network; users never receive broad IP-level access to internal subnets

explains continuous verification: authenticates and authorizes every single request based on user identity, device posture, location, and behavioral context via identity-aware proxies (e.g. BeyondCorp)
